items.title: Location, Size & Extent of India
items.body:
## In one line
Where India sits on the globe, how big it is, and the exact points and neighbours that define its edges.

## Why it is asked
Location, the IST meridian, the area rank and the longest/shortest land borders are classic single-fact prelims questions.

## The story
- India lies between **8°4' N and 37°6' N** latitude and **68°7' E and 97°25' E** longitude, in South Asia.
- The **Tropic of Cancer (23½° N)** cuts the country into near-equal halves and passes through **8 states**: Gujarat, Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, West Bengal, Tripura and Mizoram.
- **Indian Standard Time** is fixed on the **82°30' E** meridian (near Mirzapur), making the clock **5 hours 30 minutes ahead of GMT**. Because India spans about 30° of longitude, the sun actually rises about 2 hours earlier in the east than in the west.
- India is the **7th-largest** country by area (**3.287 million km²**), the largest in South Asia; it runs **3,214 km** north–south and **2,933 km** east–west.
- Its land boundary is about **15,200 km** and its coastline **7,516.6 km** (Arabian Sea to the west, Bay of Bengal to the east).

## Picture it — the extremities
- **Northernmost:** Indira Col (near the Siachen Glacier).
- **Southernmost:** Indira Point (Great Nicobar).

## Neighbours by land-border length

| Neighbour | Border (km) |
|---|---|
| Bangladesh | 4,096 (longest) |
| China | 3,488 |
| Pakistan | 3,323 |
| Nepal | 1,751 |
| Myanmar | 1,643 |
| Bhutan | 699 |
| Afghanistan | 106 (shortest) |

## Terms explained
- **Meridian** = a line of longitude; IST uses the 82°30' E meridian as the single reference clock for the whole country.
- **Indira Col vs Indira Point** = the far north point vs the far south point — same name, opposite ends.

## Don't confuse
- **Indira Col (north) vs Indira Point (south)** — the exam deliberately swaps these.
- **Westernmost longitude (68°7' E) is not the IST meridian** — IST is 82°30' E.

## Remember it
Border order "**BaChiPaNeMyBhA**" = Bangladesh > China > Pakistan > Nepal > Myanmar > Bhutan > Afghanistan.

## TL;DR
- India: 8°4'–37°6' N and 68°7'–97°25' E; Tropic of Cancer through 8 states.
- IST is based on 82°30' E, 5 h 30 min ahead of GMT.
- 7th-largest country (3.287 million km²); coastline 7,516.6 km, land border about 15,200 km.
- Northernmost = Indira Col; southernmost = Indira Point (Great Nicobar).
- Longest land border with Bangladesh (4,096 km); shortest with Afghanistan (106 km).

items.title: The Himalayas — Ranges, Peaks & Regional Divisions
items.body:
## In one line
The Himalayas are young, still-rising fold mountains arranged in parallel ranges from north to south, and in belts from west to east.

## Why it is asked
Matching a range to its description, naming the highest peak wholly in India, and identifying the Purvanchal hills are repeat prelims items.

## The story — ranges from north to south
- **Trans Himalaya** — the Karakoram, Ladakh, Zanskar and Kailash ranges on the Tibetan side; K2 (8,611 m) stands here.
- **Great Himalaya / Himadri** — the loftiest, continuous, permanently snow-covered range with a granite core (average about 6,000 m). Peaks: Everest (in Nepal), **Kanchenjunga 8,586 m (the highest peak in India, on the Sikkim–Nepal border; Nanda Devi 7,816 m is the highest lying wholly within India)**, Nanga Parbat, Nanda Devi, Namcha Barwa.
- **Lesser Himalaya / Himachal** — 3,700–4,700 m; the **Pir Panjal** (longest), Dhauladhar and Mahabharat ranges; holds the Kashmir, Kullu and Kangra valleys and the hill stations.
- **Shiwalik / Outer Himalaya** — 900–1,100 m of loosely packed river sediment; flat-floored valleys called **Duns** (such as Dehra Dun) lie between the Shiwalik and the Lesser Himalaya.

## The story — belts from west to east
Kashmir (Karewa saffron soils, cold desert) → Himachal and Uttarakhand → Darjeeling–Sikkim (the Tista; no Shiwalik here) → Arunachal (Namcha Barwa, deep gorges) → **Purvanchal**, the eastern hills (Patkai, Naga, Manipur and Mizo/Lushai hills) that form India's eastern boundary.

Being **young fold mountains that are still rising**, the Himalayas give India antecedent rivers and deep gorges.

**Four Himalayan passes to know**

| Pass | Where / what it connects |
|---|---|
| Zoji La | connects Srinagar (Kashmir Valley) with the Indus/Ladakh side |
| Khardung La | gateway to the Nubra Valley, Ladakh |
| Karakoram Pass | India–China route on the Karakoram Range |
| Nathu La | India–China trade pass in Sikkim (trade reopened in 2006) |

## Terms explained
- **Fold mountains** = ranges formed when crust is squeezed and buckled upward (here, India colliding with Asia).
- **Dun** = a flat valley between the Shiwalik and the Lesser Himalaya.
- **Purvanchal** = the eastern hill arc where the Himalayas bend south.

## Don't confuse
- **Himadri (Greater) vs Trans Himalaya:** Himadri holds Kanchenjunga; the Trans Himalaya holds the Karakoram and K2.
- **Highest in the world (Everest, Nepal) vs highest in India (Kanchenjunga, on the Nepal border) vs highest wholly within India (Nanda Devi).**

## Remember it
Ranges north→south "**TG-LS**" = Trans, Greater (Himadri), Lesser (Himachal), Shiwalik.

## TL;DR
- North→south ranges: Trans Himalaya, Himadri (Greater), Himachal (Lesser), Shiwalik (Outer).
- Kanchenjunga (8,586 m) is the highest peak in India; Nanda Devi (7,816 m) is the highest lying wholly within India.
- Pir Panjal is the longest Lesser-Himalaya range; Duns lie between the Shiwalik and the Lesser Himalaya.
- West→east: Kashmir → Himachal-Uttarakhand → Darjeeling-Sikkim → Arunachal → Purvanchal.
- Purvanchal = Patkai, Naga, Manipur and Mizo (Lushai) hills.

items.title: Northern Plains & the Peninsular Plateau
items.body:
## In one line
Two very different lowlands and uplands: the young, flat, river-built Northern Plains, and the ancient, hard-rock Peninsular Plateau.

## Why it is asked
The north-to-south belts of the plains and the position of the Central Highlands, Deccan, Vindhya and Satpura relative to the Narmada are frequent statement-and-match questions.

## The story — the Northern Plains
- Built from the alluvium (river silt) of the **Indus, Ganga and Brahmaputra**; about 7 lakh km² and roughly 2,400 km long.
- Three sections: **Punjab Plains** (Indus system), **Ganga Plains** (Ghaggar to Teesta) and **Brahmaputra Plains** (Assam).
- From north to south a river crosses four relief belts: **Bhabar** (a narrow pebbly strip where streams sink underground) → **Terai** (a marshy belt where they re-emerge) → **Bhangar** (older alluvium with lime nodules called kankar) → **Khadar** (younger, yearly-renewed, most fertile floodplain).

## The story — the Peninsular Plateau
- India's **oldest and largest** division (600–900 m), an irregular triangle of ancient crystalline, igneous and metamorphic rock left from the break-up of the **Gondwana** landmass. The **Deccan Trap** is thick basaltic lava that weathers into black soil.
- **Central Highlands** lie **north of the Narmada** (Malwa, Bundelkhand, Chotanagpur).
- **Deccan Plateau** lies **south of the Narmada** and tilts east; drained by the Godavari, Krishna and Kaveri.
- The **Vindhya** (north of the Narmada) and the **Satpura** (between the Narmada and the Tapi; highest point Dhupgarh, 1,350 m) form the divide between north and south India.
- Edged by the **Western Ghats** (continuous, higher) and the **Eastern Ghats** (broken, cut by rivers).

**Western vs Eastern Ghats**

| Feature | Western Ghats | Eastern Ghats |
|---|---|---|
| Height and form | higher and more continuous | lower, discontinuous, dissected by the major east-flowing rivers (Godavari, Krishna) |
| Highest peak | Anaimudi (2,695 m) — highest peak of peninsular India | Arma Konda (about 1,680 m), Andhra Pradesh |

The two Ghats meet at the **Nilgiri Hills** in the south.

## Terms explained
- **Alluvium** = fine silt dropped by rivers; it makes the plains so fertile.
- **Kankar** = hard calcium-carbonate nodules found in the older Bhangar soil.
- **Gondwana** = the ancient southern supercontinent India once belonged to.

## Don't confuse
- **Bhangar (old) vs Khadar (new):** Bhangar is higher, older, with kankar; Khadar is the fresh, fertile floodplain.
- **Central Highlands are north of the Narmada; the Deccan is south of it** (easy to flip).
- **Vindhya (north of Narmada) vs Satpura (Narmada–Tapi).**

## Remember it
Plains belts north→south "**BT-BK**" = Bhabar, Terai, Bhangar, Khadar.

## TL;DR
- Northern-Plains belts north→south: Bhabar → Terai → Bhangar → Khadar (Khadar most fertile).
- Plains built by Indus, Ganga and Brahmaputra alluvium; three sections Punjab/Ganga/Brahmaputra.
- The Peninsular Plateau is India's oldest and largest division, from the Gondwana landmass.
- Central Highlands lie north of the Narmada; the Deccan Plateau lies south of it.
- Vindhya (north of Narmada) and Satpura (Narmada–Tapi) form the divide; Western Ghats continuous, Eastern Ghats discontinuous.

items.title: Coastal Plains, Islands & the Thar Desert
items.body:
## In one line
India's two coastal plains have opposite personalities, and its two island groups have opposite origins.

## Why it is asked
Submergent vs emergent coasts, and volcanic vs coral islands, are reliable discrimination questions.

## The story — the coastal plains (about 6,000 km)

| Feature | Western Coastal Plain | Eastern Coastal Plain |
|---|---|---|
| Lies between | Western Ghats and the Arabian Sea | Eastern Ghats and the Bay of Bengal |
| Coast type | **Submergent** (land sank — gives natural harbours) | **Emergent** (land rose — broad and deltaic) |
| Width | Narrow (about 65 km) | Wider |
| Segments | Kutch, Konkan, Karnataka (Kanara), Malabar (Kerala) | Northern Circars, Coromandel |

- The two plains meet at **Kanyakumari**. The deep, sheltered west coast makes good ports; the wide east coast carries the big deltas of the Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna and Cauvery.

## The story — the islands
- **Andaman & Nicobar** (Bay of Bengal) are of **volcanic / tectonic** origin and include **Barren Island**, India's only active volcano; **Indira Point** on Great Nicobar is the southern tip.
- **Lakshadweep** (Arabian Sea) is of **coral** origin — low-lying atolls.

## The story — the Thar Desert
The **Great Indian (Thar / Marusthali) Desert** spans Rajasthan and Gujarat; the **Great Rann of Kutch** (Gujarat) is a salt-soaked seasonal wetland; the seasonal **Luni** is its main river.

## Terms explained
- **Submergent coast** = a coast where the land sank (or the sea rose), drowning valleys to form natural harbours.
- **Emergent coast** = a coast where the land rose, giving a wide, smooth, often deltaic plain.
- **Atoll** = a ring-shaped coral reef and island enclosing a lagoon.

**The east coast, segment by segment — and Andhra Pradesh**
The **Northern Circars** run along Odisha and Andhra Pradesh; the **Coromandel Coast** runs along **Tamil Nadu** and holds the **Cauvery delta**. Andhra Pradesh itself combines three landforms: the **eastern margin of the Deccan plateau**, the **Eastern Ghats**, and an **emergent east coast** built by the **Godavari–Krishna deltas**.

## Don't confuse
- **Western = submergent (harbours); Eastern = emergent (deltas)** — easy to reverse.
- **Andaman & Nicobar = volcanic/tectonic; Lakshadweep = coral** — not the other way round.

## Remember it
"**West sank to make harbours; East rose to make deltas. Andaman burns (volcano); Lakshadweep grows (coral).**"

## TL;DR
- Western coast is submergent (good harbours); eastern coast is emergent, wider and deltaic.
- West-coast segments: Kutch, Konkan, Kanara, Malabar; east-coast: Northern Circars, Coromandel.
- Andaman & Nicobar are volcanic/tectonic (Barren Island active volcano); Lakshadweep is coral.
- The two coastal plains meet at Kanyakumari.
- The Thar Desert lies in Rajasthan/Gujarat; the Great Rann of Kutch is a salt marsh in Gujarat.

items.title: Drainage — Himalayan vs Peninsular River Systems
items.body:
## In one line
India's rivers split into two families — snow-fed Himalayan rivers that flow all year, and rain-fed Peninsular rivers that are mostly seasonal.

## Why it is asked
Which rivers form the Panchnad, which flow west, and what "antecedent" means are standard prelims facts.

## The story — key ideas
- A **drainage basin** is the whole area a river and its tributaries drain; the **watershed** is the high boundary dividing two basins.
- An **antecedent river** is older than the mountains it crosses — it kept its course and cut a gorge as the land rose. The Indus, Sutlej and Brahmaputra do this across the Himalayas.

## The story — Himalayan rivers (perennial)
- **Indus** — rises near Lake Mansarovar in Tibet (called 'Singi Khamban'); its five Punjab tributaries (Jhelum, Chenab, Ravi, Beas, Satluj) unite as the **Panchnad**; inside India it flows only through Leh (Ladakh).
- **Ganga** — about 2,525 km; main tributaries the Yamuna, Ghaghara, Gandak, Kosi (the 'Sorrow of Bihar') and Son.
- **Brahmaputra** — rises in Tibet as the Tsangpo, enters through Arunachal (as the Dihang); braided and heavily silt-laden.

## The story — Peninsular rivers (mostly seasonal)
- **East-flowing** into the Bay of Bengal, forming deltas: **Godavari** (the largest, 'Dakshin Ganga'), **Krishna**, **Kaveri**, **Mahanadi**.
- **West-flowing** into the Arabian Sea through rift valleys, forming estuaries not deltas: **Narmada** and **Tapi**.

**Drainage patterns**

| Pattern | What it looks like |
|---|---|
| Dendritic | tree-like branching pattern developed on rocks of uniform resistance (the Ganga plains) |
| Trellis | rectangular pattern on tilted or folded strata, with tributaries joining at right angles |
| Radial | streams flow outward in all directions from a central dome or volcano (Amarkantak) |
| Centripetal | streams converge inward into a central basin or depression |

**Four record lakes**

| Lake | Record |
|---|---|
| Wular | largest freshwater lake of India, in Jammu & Kashmir (a tectonic lake) |
| Chilika | largest brackish-water coastal lagoon of India, in Odisha |
| Sambhar | largest inland salt-water lake of India, in Rajasthan |
| Kolleru | freshwater lake between the Krishna and Godavari deltas, Andhra Pradesh |

## Terms explained
- **Perennial** = flowing all year (fed by snowmelt plus rain).
- **Panchnad** = the "five rivers" of Punjab joined together before meeting the Indus.
- **Estuary vs delta** = a single widening river mouth (estuary) versus a fan of distributaries (delta).

**Waterfalls and dams — which river?**

| Waterfall / dam | River | State |
|---|---|---|
| Jog (Gersoppa) Falls | Sharavati | Karnataka (India's best-known plunge waterfall) |
| Nagarjuna Sagar Dam | Krishna | Andhra Pradesh–Telangana border |
| Sardar Sarovar Dam | Narmada | Gujarat |
| Hirakud Dam | Mahanadi | Odisha (one of the longest earthen dams) |

## Don't confuse
- **Narmada and Tapi flow WEST**; all the other major peninsular rivers flow east.
- **Antecedent (older than the uplift) vs consequent (follows the new slope)** rivers.

## Remember it
West-flowing peninsular pair = "**NT**" (Narmada, Tapi); every other major flows east.

## TL;DR
- Himalayan rivers are perennial and antecedent; peninsular rivers are mostly rain-fed and seasonal.
- The Indus's five Punjab tributaries (Jhelum, Chenab, Ravi, Beas, Satluj) form the Panchnad.
- The Godavari is the largest peninsular river ('Dakshin Ganga'); the Kosi is the 'Sorrow of Bihar'.
- East-flowing peninsular rivers (Godavari, Krishna, Kaveri, Mahanadi) build deltas in the Bay of Bengal.
- Narmada and Tapi flow west through rift valleys into the Arabian Sea, forming estuaries not deltas.

items.title: Indian Monsoon & Climate
items.body:
## In one line
The monsoon is a giant seasonal sea-breeze that reverses twice a year, bringing India most of its rain and deciding the farming year.

## Why it is asked
The onset mechanism (Tibetan low, jet streams), the role of the retreating monsoon for the Coromandel coast, and El Niño/IOD effects are regularly tested.

## The story — the mechanism
- 'Monsoon' comes from the Arabic **mausim** (season): winds that reverse direction — sea to land in summer, land to sea in winter.
- **South-west monsoon (June–September):** an intense **low-pressure area over the heated Tibetan Plateau**, the **northward shift of the Subtropical Jet Stream (STJ)** away from the Himalayas, the forming of the **Tropical Easterly Jet (TEJ)**, and the **Somali (Findlater) Jet** together trigger onset — over Kerala around the first week of June.
- The flow splits into the **Arabian Sea** and **Bay of Bengal** branches; a mid-season **'break'** gives dry spells.
- **North-east / retreating monsoon (October–December):** high pressure rebuilds over Tibet/Siberia and the rain belt shifts south; winds cross the Bay of Bengal to drench the **Coromandel coast (Tamil Nadu)** and coastal Andhra Pradesh — their main rainy season.

## The story — year-to-year controls
- **El Niño** (a warm central/eastern Pacific) tends to **weaken** the south-west monsoon; **La Niña** strengthens it.
- A **positive Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD)** favours a good monsoon.

## Terms explained
- **Jet stream** = a fast, narrow ribbon of high-altitude wind; the STJ's seasonal shift gates the monsoon's start.
- **ITCZ** = the equatorial rain belt that migrates north in summer and south in winter.
- **IOD** = the Indian Ocean Dipole, a see-saw of sea-surface temperatures across the Indian Ocean.

## Don't confuse
- **South-west monsoon (June–Sept) vs north-east/retreating monsoon (Oct–Dec)** — the latter is what waters the Coromandel coast.
- **El Niño weakens, La Niña and a positive IOD strengthen** the monsoon.

## Remember it
"**Tibet heats up → jet jumps north → monsoon bursts over Kerala in June.**"

## TL;DR
- SW-monsoon onset is driven by the Tibetan low, the northward shift of the Subtropical Jet Stream and the Tropical Easterly Jet.
- The SW monsoon (June–Sept) has Arabian Sea and Bay of Bengal branches; onset over Kerala about the first week of June.
- The NE (retreating) monsoon brings the main rainfall to the Coromandel coast and coastal Andhra Pradesh.
- El Niño generally weakens the SW monsoon; La Niña and a positive IOD strengthen it.
- 'Monsoon' comes from the Arabic 'mausim', meaning season.

items.title: Soils & Natural Vegetation of India
items.body:
## In one line
India's soils and the natural plants that grow on them follow the rainfall and the parent rock — so soil, climate and vegetation form one linked story.

## Why it is asked
Soil-to-crop matching and the rainfall ladder of forest types are dependable prelims questions.

## The story — soils (ICAR groups 8 types)

| Soil | Where it forms | Crops / notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Alluvial** | Indo-Gangetic-Brahmaputra plain and deltas | India's most extensive (about 43%); potash-rich, phosphorus-poor; wheat, rice, sugarcane |
| **Black (Regur)** | the Deccan Trap | cotton; moisture-retentive and self-ploughing; rich in lime and iron, poor in nitrogen and phosphorus |
| **Red** | low-rainfall crystalline areas | red from iron oxide; millets, pulses |
| **Laterite** | high heat with heavy rain uplands | heavily leached, low in humus; cashew, ragi, tea |
| **Desert** | arid Rajasthan and Gujarat | salty, wind-blown; bajra and barley with irrigation |

(There are also forest/mountain, saline-alkaline and marshy soils.)

## The story — natural vegetation (by rainfall and height)
- **Tropical evergreen** (over 200 cm rain): Western Ghats, the north-east, the Andamans — rosewood, mahogany, ebony.
- **Deciduous / monsoon** (100–200 cm): the **most widespread** — teak and sal.
- **Dry deciduous / thorn** (under 100 / under 50 cm): central India, Rajasthan — acacia, babul.
- **Tidal (mangrove):** river deltas — the Ganga Sundarbans (the **Sundari** tree), Godavari, Krishna, Mahanadi, Cauvery.
- **Mountain / alpine:** conifers (pine, fir, oak) grading up to alpine grasses above the tree line.
- The 1988 Forest Policy target is **33%** of the area under forest.

## Terms explained
- **Leaching** = heavy rain washing minerals downward, leaving laterite poor and iron-rich.
- **Regur** = the local name for black cotton soil of the Deccan.
- **Deciduous** = trees that shed their leaves in the dry season.

## Don't confuse
- **Red vs laterite:** red soil forms in low rainfall on crystalline rock; laterite forms under heavy rain by leaching.
- **Evergreen needs the MOST rain (over 200 cm); thorn the least (under 50 cm).**

## Remember it
"Regur = **Deccan + cotton + self-ploughing cracks.**"

## TL;DR
- ICAR classifies Indian soils into 8 groups; alluvial soil is the most extensive (about 43%).
- Black (Regur) soil on the Deccan Trap is ideal for cotton and self-ploughs when dry.
- Laterite soil forms by heavy leaching under high heat and rainfall; low in humus.
- Vegetation shifts with rainfall: evergreen (over 200 cm) → deciduous → thorn (under 50 cm); teak dominates monsoon forests.
- Sundari is the key mangrove tree of the Sundarbans; the 1988 Forest Policy targets 33% forest cover.

items.body:
## In one line
How India's forests are classified, which forest type covers the most ground, and where its signature wild animals survive.

## Why it is asked
Champion & Seth group numbers, the "first/largest" park facts, and animal-to-habitat matching are repeat prelims items.

## The story — forest types (Champion & Seth)
India's forests are grouped into **5 major groups** and **16 type-groups**; the mix changes with **rainfall** and **altitude**.

| Type | Rainfall | Trees |
|---|---|---|
| Tropical evergreen | over 200 cm | rosewood, mahogany, ebony |
| Tropical moist deciduous | 100–200 cm | **sal**, teak, sandalwood |
| Tropical dry deciduous | 70–100 cm | **teak**, bamboo |
| Thorn and scrub | under 70 cm | acacia (kikar), khair |
| Tidal (mangrove) | deltas / estuaries | sundari |

- **Tropical deciduous (monsoon) forests are the most widespread** in India.
- Mountain forests grade from oak and pine, through deodar and silver fir, up to alpine meadows.

## The story — wildlife conservation
- **Jim Corbett** (formerly Hailey, **1936**) was India's **first national park**.
- **Project Tiger** was launched in **1973** (9 reserves) and is run by the **NTCA**; **Nagarjunasagar-Srisailam** is the largest tiger reserve by area.
- **Hemis** (Ladakh) is India's **largest national park**; **Madhya Pradesh** has the highest tiger population (the 'Tiger State').

## Picture it — signature strongholds

| Animal | Stronghold |
|---|---|
| Asiatic Lion | Gir National Park, Gujarat |
| One-horned Rhinoceros | Kaziranga National Park, Assam |
| Asiatic Wild Ass | Little Rann of Kutch |
| Hangul (Kashmir stag) | Dachigam National Park, J&K |
| Great Indian Bustard | Desert NP (Rajasthan), Rollapadu (AP) |

## Terms explained
- **Champion & Seth** = the authors of India's standard forest-type classification.
- **NTCA** = National Tiger Conservation Authority, which runs Project Tiger.
- **Endemic** = found naturally in only one place (the Hangul is endemic to Dachigam).

## Don't confuse
- **Sal (moist deciduous) vs teak (dry deciduous)** — different rainfall bands.
- **First national park (Corbett) vs largest national park (Hemis).**

## Remember it
Forest rainfall ladder "**Ever-Moist-Dry-Thorn**" = over 200 / 100 / 70 / under 70 cm.

## TL;DR
- Champion & Seth classify Indian forests into 5 major groups and 16 type-groups.
- Tropical deciduous (monsoon) forests are the most widespread; sal = moist deciduous, teak = dry deciduous.
- Tropical evergreen forests need over 200 cm rainfall; thorn/scrub grows below 70 cm.
- Jim Corbett (1936) was India's first national park; Project Tiger began in 1973.
- Hemis (Ladakh) is India's largest national park; Madhya Pradesh has the highest tiger population.
- Asiatic Lion = Gir; one-horned Rhino = Kaziranga; Asiatic Wild Ass = Little Rann of Kutch; Hangul = Dachigam.

## In one line
A revision cluster of the exact named-entity matches that UPSC and APPSC repeatedly test — learn the pairs and the traps.

## Why it is asked
Match-the-following and multi-statement questions hinge on these precise glacier–river, peak–region, river–basin and island facts.

## Glacier → river it feeds

| Glacier | River | Trap |
|---|---|---|
| Gangotri (Gaumukh) | Bhagirathi (Ganga) | — |
| Bandarpunch | Yamuna | — |
| Bara Shigri | Chenab | — |
| Milam | **Goriganga** | NOT Mandakini |
| Zemu | **Teesta** | NOT Manas |
| Siachen | Nubra | India's largest glacier |

## Peaks and hills → location
- **Namcha Barwa** → Arunachal (East Himalaya), **not Garhwal**; **Nanda Devi** → Kumaon; **Nokrek** → Meghalaya (Garo Hills), **not Sikkim**.
- **Cardamom Hills** → southern Western Ghats; **Kaimur** → the Vindhyan range; **Mahadeo** → the Satpura range; **Mikir (Karbi Anglong)** → Assam (north-east).

## Rivers
- **Godavari** tributaries: **Indravati, Pranahita** (Wardha plus Wainganga), Manjira, Sabari. The **Pennar** and the **Vamsadhara** are independent rivers (not Godavari/Krishna tributaries).
- **Nagavali and Vamsadhara** rise in the **Eastern Ghats** (north-coastal AP/Odisha). The **Teesta**'s main tributary is the **Rangeet**.
- Indus: the five Punjab rivers form the **Panchnad**, which the **Chenab** carries to join the Indus.

**Where four big rivers rise**

| River | Source |
|---|---|
| Ganga (as the Bhagirathi) | Gangotri Glacier (Gaumukh), Uttarakhand |
| Godavari | Trimbak near Nashik, Western Ghats |
| Krishna | Mahabaleshwar, Western Ghats |
| Narmada | Amarkantak Plateau (Madhya Pradesh) — it flows west through a rift valley |

## Islands and spread
- The **Ten Degree Channel** separates the **Andaman** group from the **Nicobar** group; **Great Nicobar** is closest to **Sumatra**; **Indira Point** is India's southernmost point.
- The **Himalayas** span **more than five** states; the **Western Ghats** span **six** (Gujarat, Maharashtra, Goa, Karnataka, Kerala, Tamil Nadu); **Pulicat** spans **AP and Tamil Nadu**.
- **Easternmost state = Arunachal Pradesh; westernmost = Gujarat.**
- **Tea-growing states:** Assam (largest), West Bengal, Tamil Nadu, Kerala, plus Himachal, Tripura and (Araku) Andhra Pradesh.

## Terms explained
- **Tributary** = a smaller river that joins a larger one; an **independent river** reaches the sea on its own.
- **Channel** = a sea strait; the Ten Degree Channel runs along the 10° N line.

## Don't confuse
- **Milam → Goriganga (not Mandakini); Zemu → Teesta (not Manas)** — the two traps examiners love.
- **Pennar and Vamsadhara are independent**, not Godavari/Krishna tributaries.

## Remember it
"**Milam–Gori, Zemu–Teesta**" — fix the two glacier traps first.

## TL;DR
- Glacier→river: Bandarpunch→Yamuna, Bara Shigri→Chenab, Milam→Goriganga (not Mandakini), Zemu→Teesta (not Manas), Siachen→Nubra.
- Namcha Barwa is in Arunachal (not Garhwal); Nokrek in Meghalaya (not Sikkim); Nanda Devi in Kumaon.
- Godavari tributaries include Indravati and Pranahita; Pennar and Vamsadhara are independent; Nagavali & Vamsadhara rise in the Eastern Ghats.
- Ten Degree Channel separates Andaman from Nicobar; Great Nicobar is closest to Sumatra; Indira Point is the southernmost point.
- Himalayas span more than five states; Western Ghats span six; Pulicat spans AP and Tamil Nadu; easternmost state = Arunachal, westernmost = Gujarat.
- Tea-growing states: Assam (largest), West Bengal, Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Himachal Pradesh, Tripura and Andhra Pradesh (Araku).

items.title: Location Detail — Area Rank, Extremities, Neighbours & Border States
items.body:
### Location Detail — Area Rank, Extremities, Neighbours & Border States

**In one line**
India is the **7th-largest** country (about **2.4%** of the world's land), and exam questions on location mostly ask for an extreme point, the IST states, or which states touch which neighbour.

**The story**
India is the **seventh-largest** country and has **28 states and 8 Union Territories**; the **Tropic of Cancer** crosses **eight** of its states. It is larger than the **European Union** but smaller than Russia, Canada, the USA, China, Brazil and **Australia**. Because it spans about 30° of longitude, local time differs by about **two hours** between Arunachal and Gujarat; that is why one standard meridian (82°30' E) is used. The **82°30' E** meridian runs through five states — **Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Odisha and Andhra Pradesh**. **Ujjain** lies close to the Tropic of Cancer. At sea India meets **Sri Lanka** (across the **Palk Strait** and Gulf of Mannar) and the **Maldives**.

| Extreme point | Place |
|---|---|
| Northernmost | **Indira Col** (Karakoram, Siachen area, Ladakh) |
| Southernmost (whole country) | Indira Point (Great Nicobar) |
| Southernmost (mainland) | **Kanyakumari** (Cape Comorin) |
| Easternmost | **Kibithu** (Arunachal Pradesh) |
| Westernmost | **Guhar Moti** (Sir Creek area, Kutch, Gujarat) |

**States on each land border**

| Neighbour | Indian states / UTs touching it |
|---|---|
| **China** | Ladakh, **Himachal Pradesh**, **Uttarakhand**, Sikkim, Arunachal Pradesh |
| **Nepal** | Uttarakhand, Uttar Pradesh, **Bihar**, West Bengal, **Sikkim** (5) |
| **Bhutan** | Sikkim, **West Bengal**, **Assam**, Arunachal Pradesh (4) |
| **Bangladesh** | West Bengal, Assam, **Meghalaya**, **Tripura**, Mizoram (5) |
| **Myanmar** | Arunachal Pradesh, **Nagaland**, **Manipur**, Mizoram (4) |
| **Pakistan** | Gujarat, **Rajasthan**, **Punjab**, Jammu & Kashmir, Ladakh |

**Don't confuse**
Southernmost point of India = Indira Point (an island); southernmost point of the mainland = Kanyakumari. Sikkim touches three countries (China, Nepal, Bhutan); Arunachal touches three (China, Bhutan, Myanmar).

**TL;DR**
- 7th-largest country, about 2.4% of world land; 28 states + 8 UTs.
- IST meridian 82°30' E crosses UP, MP, Chhattisgarh, Odisha and Andhra Pradesh.
- Extremes: Indira Col (N), Indira Point (S), Kanyakumari (S mainland), Kibithu (E), Guhar Moti (W).
- Nepal 5 states; Bangladesh 5; Bhutan 4; Myanmar 4; China 5 (incl. Ladakh); Pakistan 4 + Ladakh.
keyPoints: India occupies about 2.4% of the world's land area and is the 7th-largest country.
The 82°30' E meridian passes through UP, MP, Chhattisgarh, Odisha and Andhra Pradesh.
Easternmost point Kibithu (Arunachal); westernmost Guhar Moti (Gujarat); southernmost mainland point Kanyakumari.
States bordering Bangladesh: West Bengal, Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, Mizoram.
States bordering Myanmar: Arunachal Pradesh, Nagaland, Manipur, Mizoram.

items.title: Himalayan & Peninsular Peaks, Regional Divisions and Duns
items.body:
### Himalayan & Peninsular Peaks, Regional Divisions and Duns

**In one line**
A peak question asks "where is it and what is it the highest of?" — and the Himalayan regions question asks which valley or deposit belongs to which belt.

**The story**
The Himalaya stretch about **2,500** km from west to east; they are about **400** km wide in Kashmir but only about **150** km in Arunachal. The **Himadri** averages about **6,000** m with asymmetric folds and a **granite** core. The Lesser Himalaya (Himachal) are **3,700**–4,700 m high and about **50 km** wide; the Shiwalik are only **10–15 km** wide, made of loose river gravels. Between the Shiwalik and the Lesser Himalaya lie the **Duns** — Dehra Dun (the largest), **Kotli** Dun and **Patli** Dun; Jammu Dun and **Pathankot** Dun lie further west.

**Peaks — where and what they top**

| Peak | Height | Where / record |
|---|---|---|
| **Everest** | 8,848 m (8,848.86 m, 2020 survey) | Nepal–Tibet; world's highest |
| **K2 (Godwin-Austen)** | 8,611 m | Karakoram (Trans Himalaya), PoK–Xinjiang; highest in India's claimed territory |
| **Kanchenjunga** | 8,586 m (source text gives 8,598 m) | Sikkim–Nepal border; highest peak in India, **third**-highest in the world |
| **Nanda Devi** | 7,816 m | Uttarakhand (Kumaon/Garhwal); highest peak lying **wholly within India** |
| **Nanga Parbat** | 8,126 m | western end of the Himadri (Gilgit-Baltistan) |
| **Namcha Barwa** | 7,782 m (source text: 7,756 m) | eastern end of the Himalaya at the **Tsangpo** bend (Tibet, beyond Arunachal) — NOT Garhwal |
| **Kamet** | 7,756 m | **Garhwal** Himalaya, Uttarakhand |
| **Makalu**, Dhaulagiri, **Annapurna** | 8,481 / 8,172 / 8,078 m | all in Nepal |
| **Saramati** | 3,826 m | Naga Hills — highest of **Nagaland** |
| **Phawngpui** (Blue Mountain) | ~2,157 m | highest of **Mizoram** |
| **Shillong Peak**; **Nokrek** | 1,961 m; 1,412 m | Meghalaya plateau (Khasi Hills); Garo Hills — NOT Sikkim |
| **Anamudi** | 2,695 m | Anaimalai Hills, **Eravikulam** NP, Kerala — highest in peninsular India |
| **Doddabetta** | 2,637 m | highest of the **Nilgiri** Hills (Tamil Nadu) |
| **Mullayanagiri** | 1,930 m | **Baba Budan** Hills — highest of Karnataka |
| **Kalsubai** | 1,646 m | highest of the northern Western Ghats (**Sahyadri**, Maharashtra) |
| **Guru Shikhar** | 1,722 m | Mount Abu — highest of the **Aravalli** (India's oldest fold mountains) |
| **Dhupgarh** | 1,350 m | Satpura range, near **Pachmarhi** (MP) |
| Vindhya high point | **752** m | low sandstone escarpment |
| **Arma Konda** (Jindhagada) | ~1,680 m | Alluri Sitharama Raju/Visakhapatnam hills, AP — highest of the **Eastern Ghats** (standard) |
| **Mahendragiri** | 1,501 m | **Odisha** — highest of the northern Eastern Ghats (our source calls it the highest overall) |
| **Agasthya**koodam | 1,868 m | Kerala–TN border; Agasthyamalai Biosphere Reserve |

**Regional divisions — the details examiners pick**

- **Kashmir Himalaya:** the Kashmir Valley lies between the Great Himalaya and the **Pir Panjal**; the Ladakh **cold desert** lies between the Great Himalaya and the Karakoram. **Karewa** deposits (glacial clay and moraine) grow **saffron**.
- **Himachal–Uttarakhand Himalaya:** from the **Ravi** to the **Kali** (a Ghaghara tributary); the Lesser Himalaya are called the **Dhauladhar** in Himachal and the **Nagtibba** in Uttarakhand.
- **Darjeeling–Sikkim Himalaya:** no Shiwalik; the **Duar** formations were developed by the British for **tea**.
- **Arunachal Himalaya:** from Bhutan to the **Diphu** Pass; peaks **Kangtu** and Namcha Barwa; the **Subansiri**, Kameng, Dihang, Dibang and **Lohit** cut deep gorges.
- **Purvanchal:** south of the **Dihang** gorge the Himalaya bend south as parallel ranges of **sandstone**.

**Don't confuse**
Kanchenjunga is the highest peak IN India (on the Nepal border); Nanda Devi is the highest lying WHOLLY within India. Arma Konda (AP) is the standard answer for the highest Eastern Ghats peak; Mahendragiri (Odisha) is the highest of the northern section. Nokrek is in Meghalaya, not Sikkim; Namcha Barwa is at the eastern end, not in Garhwal.

**TL;DR**
- Everest 8,848 m (Nepal); K2 8,611 m (Karakoram); Kanchenjunga 8,586 m (India's highest, 3rd in world); Nanda Devi 7,816 m (highest wholly in India).
- Peninsula: Anamudi 2,695 m > Doddabetta 2,637 m; Guru Shikhar 1,722 m (Aravalli); Dhupgarh 1,350 m (Satpura); Arma Konda ~1,680 m (Eastern Ghats).
- Duns: Dehra, Kotli, Patli; Karewa = saffron; Duars = tea; Nagtibba = Lesser Himalaya in Uttarakhand.
keyPoints: Kanchenjunga (8,586 m) is the highest peak in India and the third-highest in the world; Nanda Devi (7,816 m) is the highest peak wholly within India.
Anamudi (2,695 m) is the highest peak of peninsular India; Doddabetta (2,637 m) the highest of the Nilgiris.
Arma Konda (~1,680 m, Andhra Pradesh) is the highest peak of the Eastern Ghats; Mahendragiri (1,501 m) the highest in Odisha.
Guru Shikhar (1,722 m, Mount Abu) is the highest peak of the Aravalli; Dhupgarh (1,350 m) of the Satpura.
Karewa deposits of Kashmir grow saffron; the Duars of Darjeeling–Sikkim were developed for tea.

items.title: Mountain Passes of India — State by State
items.body:
### Mountain Passes of India — State by State

**In one line**
A **pass** is a low gap through a mountain range; examiners ask which state a pass is in and which two places or valleys it joins.

**The story**
Passes form where rivers, glaciers or faults cut a saddle into a range; lower ones are called hill passes or **ghats**/**gaps**. Most Himalayan passes lead from Indian valleys to Tibet; the Western Ghats gaps carry the coastal railways inland.

| Pass | State / range | Connects / note |
|---|---|---|
| **Zoji La** | Ladakh (Great Himalaya, near Dras) | Srinagar ↔ **Kargil**/Leh; BRO keeps it open; Zojila tunnel begun 2020 |
| **Banihal** | J&K (Pir Panjal) | Jammu ↔ Srinagar (Banihal–Qazigund); bypassed by the **Jawahar Tunnel** |
| **Pir Panjal Pass** | J&K | Rajouri ↔ Kashmir Valley; historic **Mughal Road** |
| **Burzil** | Kashmir (PoK) | Astore valley ↔ **Deosai** plains |
| **Pensi La** | Ladakh | Kargil (Suru) ↔ **Zanskar** |
| **Khardung La** | Ladakh (Ladakh range) | Leh ↔ **Nubra** valley; supplies to Siachen |
| **Chang La** | Ladakh | Leh ↔ **Pangong** Lake; DRDO station nearby |
| **Umling La** | Ladakh (Hanle–Chisumle) | **highest motorable** road pass in India, opened 2021 |
| **Taglang La** | Ladakh | on the **Manali–Leh** road (Debring ↔ Gya) |
| **Bara-lacha La** | Himachal–Ladakh (Zanskar range) | **Lahaul** ↔ Leh; "gateway to Ladakh"; Chandra and Bhaga rise near it |
| **Imis La** | Ladakh | Ladakh ↔ Tibet (towards **Hanle**) |
| **Lanak La** | Aksai Chin, Ladakh | Ladakh ↔ Lhasa |
| **Karakoram Pass** | Ladakh (Karakoram) | Ladakh ↔ **Xinjiang** (China); old trade route |
| **Aghil** Pass | Karakoram | north of K2; Ladakh ↔ Xinjiang |
| **Shipki La** | Himachal (Sutlej gorge) | **Kinnaur** ↔ Tibet; third trade post with China after Lipulekh and Nathu La |
| **Rohtang** | Himachal (Pir Panjal) | Kullu ↔ Lahaul–Spiti; open May–Oct; bypassed by the **Atal Tunnel** (2020); Beas rises near it |
| **Debsa** | Himachal | Kullu (**Parvati** valley) ↔ Spiti; crossed by Joydeep Sircar 1995 |
| **Lipulekh** | Uttarakhand (Pithoragarh) | India–Nepal–Tibet tri-junction; Kailash–**Mansarovar** Yatra; trade post |
| **Mana Pass** | Uttarakhand (Chamoli) | Mana ↔ Tibet; in the Nanda Devi Biosphere Reserve; snow-bound six months |
| **Niti** Pass | Uttarakhand | old Tibet route, closed since **1962** |
| **Traill**'s Pass | Uttarakhand | **Pindari** ↔ Milam valleys; very steep |
| **Mangsha Dhura** | Uttarakhand | Kuthi valley ↔ Tibet; landslide-prone |
| **Muling La** | Uttarakhand | north of **Gangotri**; seasonal |
| **Nathu La** | Sikkim | Sikkim ↔ Tibet; trade reopened **2006**; old Silk Route branch |
| **Jelep La** | Sikkim | through the **Chumbi** valley to Lhasa; closed after 1962 |
| **Bomdi La** | Arunachal Pradesh | **Arunachal** ↔ Lhasa (Tibet); east of Bhutan |
| **Diphu** | Arunachal Pradesh | India–China–Myanmar tri-junction on the **McMahon** Line |
| **Pangsau** | Arunachal Pradesh | easy route into **Myanmar** (Stilwell/Ledo road) |
| **Dihang Pass** | Arunachal Pradesh | Arunachal ↔ **Mandalay** (Myanmar) |
| **Bhor Ghat** | Maharashtra (Western Ghats) | Mumbai ↔ **Pune** (Khandala); used by the Satavahanas |
| **Thal Ghat** | Maharashtra | Mumbai ↔ **Nashik** (Kalyan–Kasara); steep railway grade |
| **Palghat** (Palakkad) Gap | Kerala–Tamil Nadu | between Nilgiris (N) and Anaimalai (S); **Coimbatore** ↔ Palakkad |
| **Shencottah** Gap | Kerala–Tamil Nadu | **Madurai** ↔ Kottayam (Kerala) |

**Don't confuse**
Zoji La (Srinagar–Kargil) vs Banihal (Jammu–Srinagar) vs Pir Panjal Pass (Mughal Road). Umling La is the highest motorable pass; Khardung La and Taglang La are often called "second highest". Nathu La is the open trade pass of Sikkim; Jelep La is closed. Bhor Ghat = Mumbai–Pune; Thal Ghat = Mumbai–Nashik.

**TL;DR**
- Ladakh/J&K: Zoji La, Banihal, Pir Panjal, Khardung La, Chang La, Umling La, Taglang La, Karakoram.
- Himachal: Shipki La, Rohtang (Atal Tunnel), Bara-lacha La; Uttarakhand: Lipulekh, Mana, Niti.
- North-east: Nathu La, Jelep La, Bomdi La, Diphu, Pangsau; Western Ghats: Bhor, Thal, Palghat, Shencottah.
keyPoints: Zoji La links Srinagar with Kargil and Leh; Banihal carries the Jammu–Srinagar road (Jawahar Tunnel).
Shipki La (Kinnaur–Tibet), Lipulekh (Uttarakhand) and Nathu La (Sikkim) are the three trade posts with China.
Rohtang links Kullu with Lahaul–Spiti and is bypassed by the Atal Tunnel (2020).
Diphu Pass is the India–China–Myanmar tri-junction; Pangsau Pass is the easy route into Myanmar.
Palghat Gap (Coimbatore–Palakkad) lies between the Nilgiri and Anaimalai hills.

items.title: The Peninsular Plateau — Sub-divisions, Ranges and Slope
items.body:
### The Peninsular Plateau — Sub-divisions, Ranges and Slope

**In one line**
The Peninsular Plateau is an old, hard-rock triangle bounded by the **Delhi Ridge**, **Rajmahal** hills, **Gir** range and Cardamom hills, divided by the Narmada into the Central Highlands and the Deccan.

**The story**
Its north-west edge is cut into the **Chambal** ravines of Bhind and **Morena** — badlands made by gully erosion. The Central Highlands (north of the Narmada) are mostly the **Malwa** plateau (500–700 m, basalt with **black soil**); eastward they narrow as **Bundelkhand** (between the Yamuna and the Vindhya, drained by the **Betwa** and **Ken**), **Baghelkhand** and the mineral-rich **Chotanagpur**. Their rivers — the Chambal, **Kali Sindh**, **Banas**, Parbati, Betwa and Ken — flow north-east to the Yamuna, which shows the slope. The **Aravalli**, India's **oldest fold** mountains, rim the plateau in the north-west.

**The Deccan and its extensions**

- The Deccan lies south of the Narmada with the Satpura at its base; the Mahadeo, Kaimur and **Maikal** ranges are its eastern arms. It **slopes** gently **eastward**, so most rivers run to the Bay of Bengal.
- It continues north-east as the Meghalaya, **Karbi**-Anglong and **North Cachar** hills. The Meghalaya plateau (**Garo**, Khasi, **Jaintia** hills) is cut off by the **Malda** (Garo–Rajmahal) gap and is known for **limestone caves**.
- Sub-plateaus: **Maharashtra** (lava, black soil), Karnataka, **Telangana** (granite, coal, limestone), the **Andhra plateau** (500–900 m; Godavari–Krishna; **bauxite**, forests) and Tamil Nadu.

| Feature | Vindhya | Satpura |
|---|---|---|
| Length | about **1,000 km** | about **800 km** |
| Rock | sandstone | granite, basalt, sandstone |
| Highest | 752 m | Dhupgarh 1,350 m |
| Role | traditional north–south **divide** | between Narmada and Tapi; forests, parks |

**Don't confuse**
Central Highlands rivers flow NORTH-EAST (to the Yamuna) even though the Deccan slopes EAST. Bundelkhand is between the Yamuna and Vindhya; Baghelkhand lies east of it.

**TL;DR**
- Plateau bounded by Delhi Ridge, Rajmahal hills, Gir range, Cardamom hills.
- Central Highlands: Malwa (black soil), Bundelkhand (Betwa, Ken), Baghelkhand, Chotanagpur; Chambal ravines in the NW.
- Deccan slopes east; extensions Maikal/Kaimur/Mahadeo; Meghalaya plateau beyond the Malda gap.
keyPoints: The Peninsular Plateau is bounded by the Delhi Ridge, Rajmahal hills, Gir range and Cardamom hills.
The Central Highlands narrow eastward as Bundelkhand, Baghelkhand and the Chotanagpur plateau.
Chambal, Kali Sindh, Banas, Betwa and Ken flow north-east, showing the slope of the Central Highlands.
The Meghalaya plateau (Garo, Khasi, Jaintia hills) is separated from the main plateau by the Malda gap.
The Aravalli are India's oldest fold mountains.

items.title: Western & Eastern Ghats — Sections, Hills and Peaks
items.body:
### Western & Eastern Ghats — Sections, Hills and Peaks

**In one line**
The **Western Ghats** are a high, continuous **escarpment** from the Tapi to Kanyakumari; the **Eastern Ghats** are older, lower and **discontinuous** hills broken by big rivers.

**The story**
The Western Ghats rose as the edge of a tilted block: a steep western face of step-like "**treppen**" and a gentle eastern slope. They run from the **Tapi** valley to **Kanyakumari** across six states, are a **UNESCO** World Heritage Site (2012) and a biodiversity **hotspot**, and their height increases from **north to south**. Because they **intercept** the south-west monsoon, Kerala and the Konkan get heavy **orographic** rain. The northern part (Tapi to **16°N**) is Deccan basalt; the central part is granite and **gneiss**. The Godavari, Krishna, Kaveri, Periyar and **Bhavani** rise here; **Silent Valley** and **Parambikulam** are biodiversity jewels.

**Local names:** **Sahyadri** (Maharashtra), Nilgiri (Karnataka–TN), Anaimalai and **Cardamom** hills (Kerala–TN).

**Western Ghats hills, north → south:** **Satmala** → **Harishchandra** → Baba Budan → Nilgiri → Anaimalai ("**elephant** mountains", with Anamudi) → Agasthyamalai → **Cardamom Hills** (the **southernmost**).

**Eastern Ghats** — **crystalline** gneiss and granite, spread over **Odisha**, Andhra Pradesh, **Telangana**, Karnataka and Tamil Nadu; rich in **bauxite** and iron ore.

| Hill range | Where |
|---|---|
| Mahendragiri | Odisha–AP border (peak 1,501 m) |
| **Simhachalam** / Kailasagiri | near **Visakhapatnam** |
| **Nallamala** | AP–Telangana, central Eastern Ghats |
| **Palkonda** | **Rayalaseema**, AP |
| **Velikonda** | granite ridges, south-eastern AP |
| Javadi, **Shevaroy** | Tamil Nadu (**Yercaud**) |

The two Ghats meet in the **Nilgiri** Hills.

**Don't confuse**
Western Ghats = continuous, higher, basalt/granite, a UNESCO site. Eastern Ghats = discontinuous, lower, crystalline, cut by the Mahanadi–Godavari–Krishna–Kaveri. Cardamom Hills are the southernmost Western Ghats range.

**TL;DR**
- Western Ghats: Tapi → Kanyakumari, 6 states, UNESCO 2012, height rises north to south.
- Hills N→S: Satmala, Harishchandra, Baba Budan, Nilgiri, Anaimalai, Agasthyamalai, Cardamom.
- Eastern Ghats in AP: Simhachalam, Nallamala, Palkonda, Velikonda; rich in bauxite.
keyPoints: The Western Ghats run from the Tapi valley to Kanyakumari and are a UNESCO World Heritage Site and biodiversity hotspot.
Western Ghats local names: Sahyadri, Nilgiri, Anaimalai and Cardamom hills; height increases north to south.
The Eastern Ghats are discontinuous crystalline hills cut by the major east-flowing rivers and are rich in bauxite.
Eastern Ghats hills of AP: Simhachalam, Nallamala, Palkonda (Rayalaseema), Velikonda.
The Western and Eastern Ghats meet in the Nilgiri Hills.

items.title: Coastal Plains — Segments, Contrasts and Ports
items.body:
### Coastal Plains — Segments, Contrasts and Ports

**In one line**
Between the Ghats and the sea lie two coastal plains about **6,000** km long: a narrow, harbour-rich west and a broad, delta-building east.

**The story**
The **Kutch** peninsula was once an **island**, joined to the mainland by Indus silt. South of it the west coast is cut into named stretches; the east coast is built of big deltas. Because west-coast rivers are short and swift they make **estuaries**, while the long east-flowing rivers make **deltas**. The east also has a wide **continental shelf**, so natural harbours are few (Kolkata is a river port). The west coast gets its rain mainly from the SW monsoon; the east gets rain from **both** the SW and NE monsoons. The Bengal coast holds the **Sundarbans**, the world's **largest mangrove** forest.

| Segment | Stretch | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Kutch & Kathiawar | Gujarat | former island; Rann salt marsh |
| **Konkan** | **Mumbai to Goa** | rocky, Mandovi and Zuari rivers |
| **Kanara** (Karnataka) | Goa to **Mangalore** | narrow, Sharavati and Netravati |
| **Malabar** | Kerala | **backwaters** (kayals), Vembanad, Periyar |
| **Utkal** | **Odisha** | Chilika lake, Mahanadi delta |
| **Northern Circars** | Mahanadi to **Krishna** | Odisha–Andhra Pradesh; Godavari–Krishna deltas |
| **Coromandel** | **Tamil Nadu** (Chennai–Cuddalore; widely, Krishna to Kanyakumari) | Cauvery delta, NE-monsoon rain |

**Ports and crops:** west — Kandla (Deendayal), Mumbai, **Mormugao**, New Mangalore, Kochi; farming is monsoon-fed coconut, **rubber** and spices. East — Kolkata–Haldia, **Paradip**, **Visakhapatnam**, Chennai, Tuticorin; deltas grow irrigated rice and **sugarcane**.

**Don't confuse**
Northern Circars (Odisha–AP) vs Coromandel (Tamil Nadu). West coast = submergent, estuaries, harbours; east coast = emergent, deltas, wide shelf.

**TL;DR**
- West: Kutch, Konkan (Mumbai–Goa), Kanara (Goa–Mangalore), Malabar (Kerala backwaters).
- East: Utkal (Odisha), Northern Circars (Mahanadi–Krishna), Coromandel (Tamil Nadu).
- West = estuaries; east = deltas, wide continental shelf, rain from both monsoons.
keyPoints: The Konkan coast runs from Mumbai to Goa; the Kanara coast from Goa to Mangalore; the Malabar coast is Kerala's.
The Northern Circars stretch from the Mahanadi to the Krishna along Odisha and Andhra Pradesh.
The Coromandel coast is the Tamil Nadu coast with the Cauvery delta.
West-coast rivers make estuaries; east-coast rivers make deltas; the east coast has a wide continental shelf.
The east coast receives rain from both the south-west and north-east monsoons.

items.title: Islands of India — Channels, Groups, Tribes and Notable Islands
items.body:
### Islands of India — Channels, Groups, Tribes and Notable Islands

**In one line**
India's islands are the volcanic-tectonic **Andaman & Nicobar** chain in the Bay of Bengal and the coral **Lakshadweep** atolls in the Arabian Sea, plus a handful of famous river and coastal islands.

**The story**
The A&N chain (about 6°45'–13°41' N) stretches about **590** km and has about **572** islands. Its capital, Port Blair, was renamed **Sri Vijaya Puram** in 2024. **Saddle Peak** (about **732** m, North Andaman) is the highest point; **Barren Island** is India's only active volcano and **Narcondam** a **dormant** one. The islands get about **3,000 mm** of rain and guard the Malacca Strait. **Great Nicobar** is the largest and southernmost Nicobar island, about **147** km from Sumatra; **Car Nicobar** has an air base; the **Nicobar pigeon** is the state bird; **Rani Jhansi** Marine NP protects Ritchie's Archipelago and **Viper** Island held a colonial prison.

| Channel | Separates |
|---|---|
| **Coco** Channel | North Andaman and the Coco Islands (**Myanmar**) |
| **Duncan** Passage | South Andaman and **Little Andaman** |
| **Ten Degree** Channel | Andaman group and **Nicobar** group |
| St. **George**'s Channel | Little Nicobar and **Great Nicobar** |
| **Grand Channel** | Great Nicobar and **Sumatra** |
| **Nine Degree** Channel | **Minicoy** and the rest of Lakshadweep |
| **Eight Degree** Channel | Minicoy and the **Maldives** |

**Tribes:** Andaman — **Jarawa**, **Sentinelese**, **Onge**, Great Andamanese (Negrito); Nicobar — **Shompen** (semi-nomadic) and **Nicobarese** (settled).

**Lakshadweep:** **36 islands**, only 10 inhabited, about **32** km² — India's smallest UT; capital **Kavaratti**; **Amindivi** islands in the north, Minicoy in the south. All are coral atolls with **fringing reefs**, just **1–2 m** above sea level, over the **Réunion** hotspot track. **Andrott** is the largest island by area (our source says Minicoy). **Mahl** (a form of **Dhivehi**) is spoken on Minicoy; **Pitti** is a bird sanctuary.

| Island | Why it is famous |
|---|---|
| **Majuli** (Assam) | world's largest **river island**; first island district (2016) |
| **Umananda** (Guwahati) | **smallest** inhabited river island |
| **Abdul Kalam** (**Wheeler**) Island | missile-testing site off Odisha |
| **Sagar Island** | Ganga Sagar Mela at **Makar Sankranti** |
| **New Moore** (South **Talpatti**) | post-1970-cyclone island disputed with Bangladesh |
| **Sriharikota** (AP) | rocket-launch barrier island between **Pulicat** Lake and the sea |
| **Rameswaram** (**Pamban**) | Gulf of Mannar, near the Palk Strait |
| **Munroe**, **Netrani**, **Diu** | Kerala lake island; Karnataka coral island; Portuguese fort island |

**Don't confuse**
Ten Degree Channel = Andaman vs Nicobar; Nine Degree = Minicoy vs Lakshadweep; Eight Degree = Minicoy vs Maldives. Barren = active volcano; Narcondam = dormant.

**TL;DR**
- A&N: ~572 islands, 590 km; capital Sri Vijaya Puram; Saddle Peak 732 m; Barren active, Narcondam dormant.
- Channels: Coco, Duncan, Ten Degree, St George's, Grand; Nine and Eight Degree in Lakshadweep.
- Lakshadweep: 36 islands, 32 km², capital Kavaratti; Majuli largest river island; Sriharikota between Pulicat and the sea.
keyPoints: The Ten Degree Channel separates the Andaman and Nicobar groups; the Duncan Passage separates South and Little Andaman.
The Nine Degree Channel separates Minicoy from Lakshadweep; the Eight Degree Channel separates Minicoy from the Maldives.
Port Blair was renamed Sri Vijaya Puram in 2024; Saddle Peak is the highest point of the A&N Islands.
Barren Island is India's only active volcano; Narcondam is dormant.
Lakshadweep has 36 islands (10 inhabited, about 32 km²); Kavaratti is the capital.

items.title: The Thar Desert (Marusthali)
items.body:
### The Thar Desert (Marusthali)

**In one line**
The **Thar** (Great Indian Desert, **Marusthali**) is a wind-shaped sandy plain **north-west of the Aravalli**, with under **150 mm** of rain.

**The story**
It covers about 2 lakh km² — about **85%** in India, mostly Rajasthan, with arms into Gujarat, Punjab and Haryana. The Aravalli form its south-eastern boundary, the Rann of Kutch its southern edge. Wind builds **barchans** (**crescent**-shaped dunes), longitudinal dunes and **mushroom** rocks; oases like Phalodi and Jaisalmer depend on groundwater. The **Luni** rises in the Aravalli near Ajmer and fades into the **Rann of Kutch**; most other streams die in **playas** (salt-lake beds) — **inland drainage**. **Akal** Wood Fossil Park near **Jaisalmer** shows the land was once forested and under the sea (Mesozoic). **Khejri** is the signature tree; the desert yields salt, gypsum and phosphate, and oil near **Barmer**.

| Feature | Detail |
|---|---|
| Rain | below 150 mm; dust storms May–June |
| River | Luni (ephemeral) |
| Fossils | Akal (Jaisalmer) |
| Minerals | gypsum, salt, oil at Barmer |

**Don't confuse**
Barchan (crescent dune, one wind direction) vs longitudinal dune (parallel to the wind). The Luni ends in the Rann, not the sea.

**TL;DR**
- Thar = Marusthali, NW of the Aravalli; 85% in India.
- Barchans, mushroom rocks, playas; Luni to the Rann of Kutch.
- Akal fossil park (Jaisalmer); oil near Barmer.
keyPoints: The Thar (Marusthali) lies north-west of the Aravalli and gets under about 150 mm of rain.
Barchans are crescent-shaped dunes made by wind from one direction.
The Luni rises in the Aravalli and ends in the Rann of Kutch.
Akal Wood Fossil Park is near Jaisalmer; oil is produced near Barmer.

items.title: Drainage — Terms, Patterns, Classification and Evolution
items.body:
### Drainage — Terms, Patterns, Classification and Evolution

**In one line**
Before memorising rivers, fix the vocabulary (catchment, basin, watershed, patterns) and the big split: **77%** of India drains to the Bay of Bengal, **23%** to the Arabian Sea.

**The story**
Flow through defined channels is **drainage**. The area a river collects water from is its **catchment area**; a **drainage basin** is everything drained by a river and its tributaries, and the line between two basins is the watershed. Watersheds are small units and basins large ones; because what happens upstream affects the whole unit, both are used as **planning regions**. The **Delhi Ridge**, the Aravalli and the **Sahyadri** form the water divide. By catchment size, major rivers drain over **20,000** km², medium ones 2,000–20,000 km² and minor ones less; the Central Water Commission lists **14 major** basins.

| Pattern | Where it forms |
|---|---|
| Dendritic | uniform rock; tree-like (Ganga plains) |
| **Trellis** | **hard and soft** rocks lying parallel; tributaries meet at right angles |
| **Rectangular** | strongly **jointed** rocky terrain |
| Radial | streams flow out from a central dome (Amarkantak) |

| Aspect | Himalayan rivers | Peninsular rivers |
|---|---|---|
| Flow | perennial (glacier + rain) | **non-perennial**, monsoon-fed |
| Type | antecedent / consequent; dendritic in plains | **superimposed**, **rejuvenated**; trellis, radial, rectangular |
| Course | young; headward erosion, river capture; meanders and shifting courses | old; **graded** profile, **fixed** course, broad shallow valleys |
| Landforms | gorges, V-valleys; meanders, **ox-bow** lakes, braided channels, deltas | low gradients, large deltas, few meanders |

**How the systems evolved**

- Himalayan: a single **Miocene** river, the Shiwalik or **Indo-Brahma**, is thought to have run from Assam to Punjab into the Gulf of Sindh. The Pleistocene uplift of the **Potwar** plateau (Delhi Ridge) split the Indus and Ganga systems, and the downfaulted **Malda gap** turned the Ganga and Brahmaputra to the Bay of Bengal.
- Peninsular: the **western flank** sank in the early Tertiary, Himalayan uplift faulted the northern edge (Narmada–Tapi troughs), and a NW–SE **tilt** sent most rivers east.

**Don't confuse**
Trellis (hard–soft parallel rocks) vs rectangular (jointed rock). Bay of Bengal drainage is 77% of the AREA, not of the water discharged.

**TL;DR**
- 77% Bay of Bengal, 23% Arabian Sea; divide = Delhi Ridge, Aravalli, Sahyadri.
- Patterns: dendritic, trellis (hard/soft), rectangular (joints), radial (dome).
- Indo-Brahma river; Potwar uplift; Malda gap. Peninsular: western-flank subsidence, NW–SE tilt.
keyPoints: About 77% of India's drainage area drains to the Bay of Bengal and 23% to the Arabian Sea.
A trellis pattern forms where hard and soft rocks lie parallel; a rectangular pattern on jointed rock.
Himalayan rivers are antecedent and young; Peninsular rivers are superimposed, rejuvenated and graded.
The Shiwalik or Indo-Brahma river is believed to have been the Miocene ancestor of the Himalayan rivers.
Peninsular drainage reflects subsidence of the western flank and a north-west to south-east tilt.

items.title: The Indus System — Source, Course, Tributaries and the Treaty
items.body:
### The Indus System — Source, Course, Tributaries and the Treaty

**In one line**
The Indus rises in Tibet, crosses Ladakh, collects the five Punjab rivers (the Panchnad) in Pakistan and enters the Arabian Sea near Karachi; the 1960 treaty splits its rivers between India and Pakistan.

**The story**
The Indus rises from a glacier near **Bokhar Chu** in the Kailash range close to Mansarovar; in Tibet it is **Singi Khamban** (Lion's Mouth). It enters India at **Demchok** and flows north-west between the Ladakh and Karakoram ranges. The **Zanskar** joins it near **Leh** and the Shyok downstream. The Panchnad joins it near **Mithankot**, and it enters the Arabian Sea near **Karachi** after about **3,180** km; the **blind** Indus dolphin lives only here. Left-bank tributaries: Zanskar, Suru, Soan and the five Punjab rivers; right-bank: Shyok, **Gilgit**, Hunza, Swat, Kurram, Gomal and **Kabul**.

| River | Source / key fact |
|---|---|
| **Chenab** (largest tributary) | **Chandra** + **Bhaga** meet near Bara-lacha La (Chandrabhaga); flows through Jammu |
| **Jhelum** | **Verinag** spring at the foot of the Pir Panjal; flows through **Wular** Lake; joins the Chenab in Pakistan |
| **Kishanganga** (**Neelum**) | largest tributary of the Jhelum |
| **Ravi** | Kullu hills / Dhauladhar, Chamba valley; **Ranjit Sagar** (Thein) dam |
| **Sutlej** | Rakas Tal near Mansarovar; antecedent, enters India at **Shipki La**; **Bhakra**–Nangal |
| **Beas** | Beas Kund near Rohtang; joins the Sutlej at **Harike** |
| **Shyok** | **Rimo** glacier; the Nubra (from the Siachen region) joins it |

**Indus Waters Treaty (1960)** — brokered by the **World Bank**: the **eastern rivers** (Ravi, Beas, Sutlej) to India, the western rivers (Indus, Jhelum, Chenab) to Pakistan, with India allowed **non-consumptive** uses (run-of-river hydropower) on the western rivers. In **April 2025**, after the Pahalgam attack, India placed the treaty "in **abeyance**".

**Don't confuse**
Eastern rivers (India) = Ravi, Beas, Sutlej; western rivers (Pakistan) = Indus, Jhelum, Chenab. Beas joins the Sutlej INSIDE India (Harike); the Jhelum joins the Chenab in Pakistan.

**TL;DR**
- Indus: Bokhar Chu (Tibet) → Demchok → Leh (Zanskar) → Mithankot (Panchnad) → Karachi.
- Chenab = Chandra + Bhaga; Jhelum from Verinag via Wular; Beas meets Sutlej at Harike.
- IWT 1960 (World Bank); in abeyance from April 2025.
keyPoints: The Indus rises near Bokhar Chu (Kailash range), is called Singi Khamban in Tibet and enters India at Demchok.
The Chenab is formed by the Chandra and Bhaga; the Jhelum rises at Verinag and flows through Wular Lake.
The Sutlej enters India through Shipki La; the Beas joins it at Harike.
The Indus Waters Treaty (1960, World Bank) gave India the Ravi, Beas and Sutlej.
India placed the Indus Waters Treaty in abeyance in April 2025.

items.title: The Ganga System — Headstreams, Panch Prayag, Tributaries
items.body:
### The Ganga System — Headstreams, Panch Prayag, Tributaries

**In one line**
The Ganga is born of many Garhwal headstreams meeting at five "prayags", enters the plains at Haridwar, gathers the Yamuna at Prayagraj and the big Nepal rivers in Bihar, and builds the world's **largest delta** with the Brahmaputra.

**The story**
The **Bhagirathi** rises at **Gaumukh**, the snout of the Gangotri glacier (about **3,892** m); the **Alaknanda** rises from the **Satopanth** and Bhagirath Kharak glaciers and passes **Badrinath**. They join at **Devprayag** to become the Ganga. At **Haridwar** the river reaches the plains and feeds the **Upper Ganga Canal**; Narora feeds the Lower Ganga Canal. The Ganga is about **2,525** km long; its basin covers about **26.4**% of India and holds nearly half the population. It flows through Uttarakhand, UP, Bihar, **Jharkhand** and West Bengal. At **Farakka** a barrage diverts water into the **Hooghly**; below it the river splits into the Bhagirathi–Hooghly and the **Padma**, which joins the Brahmaputra and **Meghna** in Bangladesh. The Ganga was declared the **National River** in **2008**.

| Prayag (confluence) | Rivers meeting |
|---|---|
| **Vishnuprayag** | **Dhauliganga** + Alaknanda |
| **Nandaprayag** | **Nandakini** + Alaknanda |
| **Karnaprayag** | **Pindar** + Alaknanda |
| **Rudraprayag** | **Mandakini** + Alaknanda |
| **Devprayag** | Alaknanda + Bhagirathi → Ganga |

| Tributary | Where it rises / joins |
|---|---|
| **Ramganga** | Dudhatoli (Chamoli); through Corbett NP; joins near **Kannauj** |
| **Yamuna** | **Yamunotri** glacier (Bandarpunch); joins at **Prayagraj**; largest Himalayan tributary the **Tons**; right-bank **Chambal**, Sind, Betwa, Ken; left-bank **Hindon** |
| **Gomti** | near Pilibhit; joins near **Ghazipur** (Sai is its tributary) |
| **Ghaghara** (Karnali) | near Mansarovar, through Nepal; joins at **Chhapra** |
| **Gandak** | Nepal (Kali Gandaki–Trisuli); joins at **Sonepur** near Patna |
| **Kosi** (**Saptakoshi**) | "Sorrow of Bihar"; joins at **Kursela** |
| **Son** | Amarkantak; the largest **south-bank** tributary, joins near Patna |

The Dhauliganga rises at **Vasundhara** Tal (**Tapovan**–Vishnugad project). Cities on the river: Rishikesh, Haridwar, Kanpur, Prayagraj, **Varanasi**, Patna, **Bhagalpur**, Kolkata.

**Don't confuse**
Order of prayags going downstream on the Alaknanda: Vishnu → Nanda → Karna → Rudra → Dev ("VNKRD"). Ghaghara joins at Chhapra, Gandak at Sonepur, Kosi at Kursela. The Son is a SOUTH-bank tributary.

**TL;DR**
- Bhagirathi (Gaumukh) + Alaknanda (Satopanth) = Ganga at Devprayag.
- Panch Prayag: Vishnu–Dhauliganga, Nanda–Nandakini, Karna–Pindar, Rudra–Mandakini, Dev.
- Yamuna at Prayagraj; Ghaghara Chhapra; Gandak Sonepur; Kosi Kursela; Son from the south.
keyPoints: The Bhagirathi rises at Gaumukh (Gangotri glacier) and meets the Alaknanda at Devprayag to form the Ganga.
Panch Prayag: Vishnuprayag (Dhauliganga), Nandaprayag (Nandakini), Karnaprayag (Pindar), Rudraprayag (Mandakini), Devprayag.
The Ghaghara joins the Ganga at Chhapra, the Gandak at Sonepur and the Kosi (Sorrow of Bihar) at Kursela.
The Son is the largest south-bank tributary of the Ganga.
The Ganga basin covers about 26.4% of India; the Ganga was declared the National River in 2008.

items.title: The Brahmaputra System — Names, Tributaries, Islands
items.body:
### The Brahmaputra System — Names, Tributaries, Islands

**In one line**
The Brahmaputra rises in Tibet as the Tsangpo, swings round Namcha Barwa into Arunachal as the Dihang (Siang), becomes the Brahmaputra in Assam and the Jamuna in Bangladesh.

**The story**
It rises from the **Chemayungdung** glacier in south-west Tibet near the Indus and Sutlej sources. As the Tsangpo ("the **Purifier**") it is gentle and navigable for about **640** km. West of **Sadiya** the Dihang is joined by the **Dibang** and Lohit and is called the Brahmaputra; it is about **2,900** km long. In Assam it is **braided**, silt-laden and flood-prone, and holds **Majuli** and **Umananda**, the largest and smallest inhabited river islands. Its basin spans Arunachal, Assam, **Meghalaya**, Nagaland, Sikkim and West Bengal; **Dibrugarh**, Pasighat, **Tezpur** and Guwahati stand on it. The Dibang reaches the plains near **Nizamghat**.

| Name | Region |
|---|---|
| Yarlung Tsangpo | Tibet |
| Dihang / **Siang** | Arunachal Pradesh |
| Brahmaputra | Assam |
| **Jamuna** | Bangladesh, then Padma–Meghna |

| Tributary | Bank / key fact |
|---|---|
| **Subansiri** | right; "**Gold River**" (gold dust); Subansiri Lower hydel |
| **Kameng** | right; rises near **Tawang** |
| **Manas** | right; from Bhutan, joins at **Jogighopa**; Manas NP |
| **Teesta** | right; from **Tso Lhamo** (Sikkim), receives the Rangeet; joins in Bangladesh |
| Sankosh, **Raidak**, Jaldhaka | right; from Bhutan/Bengal |
| **Lohit** | left; eastern Tibet through the **Mishmi** Hills |
| **Dhansiri**, **Kolong**, Burhi Dihing | left (south bank) |
| **Kopili** | largest **south-bank** tributary in Assam |

**Hydel projects:** Subansiri Lower, **Ranganadi**, Kameng (Arunachal); **Doyang** (Nagaland); Loktak (Manipur); Kopili (Assam).

**Don't confuse**
Subansiri = Gold River (Arunachal); Subarnarekha = "streak of gold" (Jharkhand–Odisha). The Teesta's tributary is the Rangeet; the Teesta is NOT fed from the Brahmaputra's source.

**TL;DR**
- Chemayungdung glacier → Tsangpo → Dihang/Siang → Brahmaputra (after Dibang + Lohit at Sadiya) → Jamuna.
- Right bank: Subansiri, Kameng, Manas, Teesta; left bank: Lohit, Dhansiri, Kopili.
- Majuli largest, Umananda smallest inhabited river island.
keyPoints: The Brahmaputra rises at the Chemayungdung glacier and is called the Tsangpo, Siang/Dihang, Brahmaputra and Jamuna along its course.
West of Sadiya the Dibang and Lohit join the Dihang to form the Brahmaputra.
The Subansiri is the "Gold River"; the Manas joins at Jogighopa; the Teesta rises at Tso Lhamo.
The Kopili is the largest south-bank tributary of the Brahmaputra in Assam.

items.title: East-flowing Peninsular Rivers — Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna, Cauvery and Others
items.body:
### East-flowing Peninsular Rivers — Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna, Cauvery and Others

**In one line**
Most Peninsular rivers rise on the **Western Ghats** (the main **water divide**) or the central plateau and flow east across the tilted Deccan into the Bay of Bengal, building deltas.

**The story**
The **Mahanadi** rises near **Pharsiya**/Sihawa in **Chhattisgarh**, runs about **851** km, is dammed at Hirakud near **Sambalpur** (a 55 km lake), passes Cuttack and reaches the sea at **False Point** near Puri; its basin hosts **Bhilai** steel and aluminium at Hirakud and **Korba**. The **Godavari** (about **1,465** km, Dakshin Ganga / **Vriddha Ganga**) rises at **Trimbak**eshwar near Nashik and drains Maharashtra, Telangana, AP, Chhattisgarh, Odisha and **Yanam**. Below Rajahmundry it splits into the **Gautami** and **Vasishta** branches, a **lobate** delta. **Marathwada** in its basin is drought-prone. The **Krishna** rises at **Mahabaleshwar** (about 1,300 m), runs about **1,400** km past Sangli, Srisailam, **Amaravati** and Vijayawada; **Rayalaseema** in its basin is drought-prone. The **Cauvery** rises at **Talakaveri** on the **Brahmagiri** range (Kodagu), runs about 800 km, and is the "**Ganga of the South**".

| River | Main tributaries | Projects |
|---|---|---|
| Mahanadi | left **Seonath**, Hasdeo, Mand, Ib; right Ong, **Tel**, Jonk | Hirakud, Gangrel, Dudhawa |
| Godavari | left Penganga, Wardha, Wainganga (→ **Pranahita**), **Indravati**, **Sabari**; right Pravara, Mula, **Manjira**, Maner | Sriram Sagar (Pochampad), **Jaikwadi**, Dowleswaram barrage, **Polavaram**, Nizam Sagar (Manjira) |
| Krishna | right Venna, **Koyna**, Panchganga, Dudhganga, **Ghataprabha**, Malaprabha, **Tungabhadra**; left **Bhima**, Dindi, **Musi**, Paleru, **Munneru** | **Almatti**, Srisailam, Nagarjuna Sagar, **Prakasam** Barrage |
| Cauvery | left Harangi, **Hemavati**, Shimsha, **Arkavati**; right Kabini, **Bhavani**, **Noyil**, Amaravati | **Krishnarajasagar**, **Mettur**, Grand Anicut |

**Tributary details:** the **Pranahita** (Wardha + **Wainganga** + Penganga) is the largest Godavari tributary; the Indravati flows through **Bastar**; the Manjira carries **Nizam Sagar**; the **Tungabhadra** (Tunga + Bhadra) passes Hospet and **Kurnool**; the Koyna dam is Maharashtra's largest **hydel** project; the Bhima rises at **Bhimashankar**; the Musi flows through **Hyderabad**; the **Panchganga** (four streams) waters **Kolhapur**; the **Kabini** comes from **Wayanad**.

**Cauvery specials:** almost **perennial** — Karnataka gets SW-monsoon rain, Tamil Nadu **NE**-monsoon rain; 90–95% of its potential is harnessed. It falls at **Sivasamudram**, narrows at **Mekedatu** (Goat's Leap) and splits round **Srirangam**. The Karnataka–TN dispute goes back to agreements of **1892** and **1924**.

| Other east-flowing river | Key facts |
|---|---|
| **Damodar** | Chotanagpur; about **541** km; joins the Hooghly; "**Sorrow of Bengal**"; tributary **Barakar**; **Damodar Valley Corporation** (1948, modelled on the **Tennessee** Valley Authority): Tilaiya, Konar, **Maithon**, Panchet; coal belt of **Jharia**, **Dhanbad**, Bokaro, Durgapur |
| **Subarnarekha** | "streak of gold"; rises near Nagri (Ranchi), about 395 km; passes **Jamshedpur**; tributary Kharkai |
| **Brahmani**, **Baitarani** | Chotanagpur rivers forming a joint delta with the Mahanadi |
| **Penner** | rises in the **Nandi** Hills (Karnataka), about 597 km, ends in Nellore district (AP); tributaries **Chitravathi**, **Papagni**, **Kunderu**, Sagileru; Somasila dam |
| Palar, **Vaigai** | Tamil Nadu (Vaigai at **Madurai**) |

**Don't confuse**
Godavari is the LONGEST Peninsular river; Mahanadi is second in water potential. Pranahita = Wardha + Wainganga (+ Penganga). The Penner is independent, not a Krishna tributary. Damodar = Sorrow of Bengal; Kosi = Sorrow of Bihar.

**TL;DR**
- Mahanadi: Chhattisgarh → Hirakud → False Point; Seonath, Hasdeo, Tel.
- Godavari: Trimbak, 1,465 km, Pranahita/Indravati/Sabari/Manjira; Gautami–Vasishta delta.
- Krishna: Mahabaleshwar, Tungabhadra/Bhima/Koyna/Musi; Cauvery: Talakaveri, Kabini/Hemavati/Bhavani, KRS–Mettur.
- Damodar (DVC 1948), Subarnarekha (Jamshedpur), Penner (Nandi Hills, Nellore).
keyPoints: The Godavari (about 1,465 km) rises at Trimbak and splits into the Gautami and Vasishta below Rajahmundry.
The Pranahita (Wardha, Wainganga, Penganga) is the largest Godavari tributary; the Indravati, Sabari and Manjira also join it.
The Krishna rises at Mahabaleshwar; the Tungabhadra is its largest tributary and the Koyna dam Maharashtra's largest hydel project.
The Cauvery rises at Talakaveri (Brahmagiri) and is nearly perennial because it gets both SW and NE monsoon rain.
The Damodar Valley Corporation (1948) was modelled on the Tennessee Valley Authority; the Penner rises in the Nandi Hills.

items.title: West-flowing Rivers — Narmada, Tapi, Mahi, Sabarmati and the Kerala Rivers
items.body:
### West-flowing Rivers — Narmada, Tapi, Mahi, Sabarmati and the Kerala Rivers

**In one line**
Only a few big Peninsular rivers flow west: the **Narmada** and **Tapi** run through **rift** valleys, and short swift streams drop off the Western Ghats — all form **estuaries**, not deltas.

**The story**
The **Narmada** rises at **Amarkantak** (Maikal range), runs about **1,312** km between the Vindhya and Satpura, cuts the Marble Rocks at **Bhedaghat** and the **Dhuandhar** falls near Jabalpur, and enters the Gulf of Khambhat by an **estuary** near **Bharuch**. Its largest tributary is the **Tawa**; others are the **Hiran**, Banjar, Shakkar, Dudhi and Burhner. The **Tapi** rises at **Multai** (Betul), runs about 724 km south of the Satpura and reaches the sea near **Surat**; its tributaries include the **Purna** and **Girna**. Both occupy **fault** (**rift**) troughs that formed when the northern Peninsula subsided during the Himalayan uplift. The **Mahi** (about 583 km) rises in the Vindhya and crosses the Tropic of Cancer **twice**. The **Sabarmati** (about 371 km) rises in the Aravalli and flows past **Ahmedabad**. The **Luni** is an **inland river** ending in the Rann.

**Western Ghats rivers:** the **Periyar** (about **244** km) is Kerala's longest (Idukki, Mullaperiyar); the **Bharathapuzha** (Nila) is second; the Sharavati makes Jog Falls; the Mandovi and **Zuari** drain Goa.

| River | Length (approx.) |
|---|---|
| Indus (overall) | 3,180 km |
| Brahmaputra (overall) | 2,900 km |
| Ganga | 2,525 km |
| Godavari | 1,465 km (longest Peninsular) |
| Krishna | 1,400 km |
| Narmada | 1,312 km (longest west-flowing) |
| Mahanadi | 851 km |
| Cauvery | 800 km |
| Tapi | 724 km |

These are the **longest** rivers in order of their quoted lengths.

**Don't confuse**
Narmada = Amarkantak, Tapi = Multai — both in MP. The Mahi crosses the Tropic of Cancer twice. The Son also rises at Amarkantak but flows NORTH-EAST to the Ganga.

**TL;DR**
- Narmada: Amarkantak → Bhedaghat/Dhuandhar → Bharuch estuary; Tawa largest tributary.
- Tapi: Multai → Surat; Mahi crosses the Tropic twice; Sabarmati past Ahmedabad.
- Periyar longest in Kerala; rift valleys explain westward flow.
keyPoints: The Narmada rises at Amarkantak and flows west through a rift valley between the Vindhya and Satpura to an estuary near Bharuch.
The Tapi rises at Multai (Betul) and reaches the sea near Surat.
The Mahi crosses the Tropic of Cancer twice; the Sabarmati rises in the Aravalli and flows past Ahmedabad.
The Periyar is Kerala's longest river.
The Narmada and Tapi occupy fault (rift) troughs, so they flow west and form estuaries.

items.body:
### Lakes of India — State, Type and Record

**In one line**
Lake questions test a record ("largest freshwater", "largest inland salt") or a type (natural, artificial, oxbow, lagoon, crater).

**The story**
Lakes form in many ways: tectonic or glacial hollows in the mountains (Wular, Gurudongmar), cut-off meanders (oxbows like Kanwar), coastal lagoons behind sandbars (Chilika, Pulicat), meteor craters (Lonar), wind-hollows filled with salt (Sambhar) and dam reservoirs (Gobind Sagar). The record lakes below are the exam favourites.

**Don't confuse**
Largest freshwater = Wular; largest coastal lagoon = Chilika; second lagoon = Pulicat; largest inland salt = Sambhar; Kolleru = natural freshwater (not artificial); Kodaikanal = artificial.

**TL;DR**
- Wular freshwater; Chilika lagoon; Pulicat 2nd lagoon; Sambhar inland salt; Kanwar oxbow; Lonar crater.
- Loktak phumdis; Vembanad longest; Kodaikanal artificial; Jaisamand 2nd artificial.
- Didwana, Kuchaman, Sargol, Khatu = Rajasthan saline lakes.
keyPoints: Wular (J&K) is India's largest freshwater lake; Sambhar (Rajasthan) the largest inland salt lake.
Chilika (Odisha) is the largest coastal lagoon; Pulicat (AP–TN) the second-largest brackish lagoon.
Kolleru, between the Godavari and Krishna deltas, is a natural freshwater lake; Kodaikanal is artificial.
Kanwar (Bihar) is Asia's largest freshwater oxbow lake; Lonar (Maharashtra) lies in a meteor crater.
Loktak (Manipur) has floating phumdis; Vembanad (Kerala) is India's longest lake.

items.title: Waterfalls of India — River and State
items.body:
### Waterfalls of India — River and State

**In one line**
Waterfall questions pair a fall with its river and state; Karnataka and Meghalaya dominate the "highest" records.

**The story**
Falls form where a river drops over a resistant rock edge — the Western Ghats escarpment, the edges of the Chotanagpur and Bastar plateaus and the Meghalaya scarp give India most of its big falls. Note the river carefully: the source text lists Kunchikal on both the Varahi and Swarna; the standard answer is the **Varahi**.

| Waterfall | River | State | Note |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Kunchikal** | **Varahi** | Karnataka | highest in India (~455 m) |
| **Jog** (Gersoppa) | Sharavati | Karnataka | **segmented**, ~253 m |
| **Nohkalikai** | Nohkalikai stream | Meghalaya (Cherrapunji) | tallest **plunge** fall |
| **Dudhsagar** | **Mandovi** | Goa–Karnataka | four-tiered "sea of milk" |
| **Athirappilly** | **Chalakudy** | Kerala | "Niagara of India" (Kerala) |
| **Chitrakote** | **Indravati** | Chhattisgarh (Bastar) | widest; "Niagara of India" |
| **Tirathgarh** | Kanger | Chhattisgarh | Kanger Valley NP |
| **Shivanasamudra**; **Hogenakkal** | Kaveri | Karnataka; Tamil Nadu | Asia's early hydel (1902) at Shivanasamudra |
| **Hundru** | **Subarnarekha** | Jharkhand (Ranchi) |  |
| **Dhuandhar** | **Narmada** | Madhya Pradesh (Jabalpur) | Marble Rocks gorge |
| **Duduma** | **Machkund** | Odisha–Andhra Pradesh | Machkund hydel |
| **Talakona** | Talakona stream | Andhra Pradesh | highest fall in AP |
| **Khandadhar**; **Barehipani** | Khandadhar; Budhabalanga | Odisha | Barehipani in Similipal |
| **Lodh** | Burha | Jharkhand | highest in Jharkhand |
| **Vantawng** | Lauvawng | Mizoram | highest in Mizoram |
| **Kakolat** | — | Bihar |  |
| **Rajat Prapat** | — | MP (Pachmarhi) |  |
| **Palaruvi** | Kallada | Kerala |  |

**Don't confuse**
Jog = Sharavati (segmented); Kunchikal = Varahi (highest overall); Nohkalikai = tallest plunge. Two "Niagaras of India": Athirappilly (Kerala) and Chitrakote (Chhattisgarh).

**TL;DR**
- Kunchikal (Varahi) highest; Jog (Sharavati) segmented; Nohkalikai tallest plunge.
- Chitrakote (Indravati), Hundru (Subarnarekha), Dhuandhar (Narmada), Duduma (Machkund).
- AP: Talakona highest; Duduma on the Odisha–AP border.
keyPoints: Kunchikal Falls on the Varahi (Karnataka) is the highest waterfall in India.
Jog Falls on the Sharavati is a segmented fall; Nohkalikai (Meghalaya) is the tallest plunge fall.
Chitrakote Falls is on the Indravati in Bastar; Hundru on the Subarnarekha near Ranchi; Dhuandhar on the Narmada.
Duduma Falls on the Machkund lies on the Odisha–Andhra Pradesh border; Talakona is AP's highest fall.
