items.title: Dams of India — River, State and Records
items.body:
### Dams of India — River, State and Records

**In one line**
Dam questions pair a dam with its river and state, or ask for a record (oldest, longest, highest, largest masonry, largest reservoir).

**The story**
A dam stores water for irrigation, power, flood control and drinking. India's oldest working one, the **Grand Anicut (Kallanai)** on the Cauvery, was built by **Karikala** Chola about the 2nd century AD to divert water over the delta. By structure, dams are gravity (Bhakra), arch (Idukki), **embankment** — earth- or rock-fill (Hirakud, Tehri) — diversion and storage dams. Our source puts the world's tallest at **Nurek** (Tajikistan).

| Dam | River | State | Note |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Grand Anicut (Kallanai)** | Cauvery | Tamil Nadu | oldest; built by **Karikala** Chola |
| **Hirakud** | Mahanadi | Odisha | **longest** dam (~25.8 km incl. dykes) |
| **Tehri** | **Bhagirathi** | Uttarakhand | highest dam (~260.5 m), rock-fill (source text wrongly says buttress) |
| **Bhakra** | Sutlej | Himachal Pradesh | highest concrete **gravity** dam (~226 m) |
| **Nagarjuna Sagar** | Krishna | AP–Telangana | largest **masonry** dam |
| **Sardar Sarovar** | **Narmada** | Gujarat | Narmada Valley Project; concrete gravity |
| **Indira Sagar** | Narmada | Madhya Pradesh | largest **reservoir** by storage |
| **Idukki** | Periyar | Kerala | double-curvature **arch** dam |
| **Mullaperiyar** | Periyar | Kerala (run by TN) | Kerala–TN dispute |
| **Pong** | **Beas** | Himachal Pradesh | Maharana Pratap Sagar |
| **Chamera**; Ranjit Sagar | **Ravi** | HP; Punjab |  |
| **Nathpa Jhakri**, Kol | Sutlej | Himachal Pradesh | SJVN hydel |
| **Salal**, **Baglihar**; Uri | Chenab; Jhelum | J&K | run-of-river |
| **Ukai**; Kadana | **Tapi**; Mahi | Gujarat |  |
| **Gandhi Sagar**, Rana Pratap Sagar, Jawahar Sagar | **Chambal** | MP; Rajasthan | Chambal Valley Project |
| **Rihand** | Rihand (Son basin) | Uttar Pradesh | **Govind Ballabh Pant** Sagar |
| **Bansagar** | **Son** | Madhya Pradesh |  |
| Tungabhadra Dam | Tungabhadra | Karnataka (**Hospet**) | shared with AP/Telangana |
| Almatti, **Narayanpur** | Krishna | Karnataka | Upper Krishna Project |
| KRS; Mettur | Cauvery | Karnataka; Tamil Nadu | Mettur = **Stanley** reservoir |
| Koyna; **Ujjani** | Koyna; Bhima | Maharashtra |  |
| Maithon; **Panchet**; Tilaiya; Konar | Barakar; **Damodar** | Jharkhand | DVC |
| **Rengali** | **Brahmani** | Odisha |  |
| **Somasila** | **Penner** (Penna) | Andhra Pradesh | Nellore district |

| **Polavaram** | Godavari | Andhra Pradesh | **national project** |
| Sriram Sagar (**Pochampad**); Nizam Sagar, **Singur** | Godavari; Manjira | Telangana |  |

**Don't confuse**
Highest = Tehri (rock-fill, Bhagirathi); highest GRAVITY = Bhakra (Sutlej); longest = Hirakud (Mahanadi); largest masonry = Nagarjuna Sagar (Krishna); largest reservoir capacity = Indira Sagar (Narmada).

**TL;DR**
- Records: Kallanai oldest, Hirakud longest, Tehri highest, Bhakra highest gravity, Nagarjuna Sagar largest masonry, Indira Sagar largest reservoir.
- Pong–Beas, Chamera–Ravi, Salal/Baglihar–Chenab, Ukai–Tapi, Gandhi Sagar–Chambal, Rihand–GB Pant Sagar.

items.title: The Monsoon in Depth — Jets, IOD, Seasons and Regional Climate
items.body:
### The Monsoon in Depth — Jets, IOD, Seasons and Regional Climate

**In one line**
India's climate is **tropical monsoon** type: seasonal winds that **reverse** with the seasons, switched on and off by the jet streams and tuned by the oceans.

**The story**
Monsoons are periodic winds that **reverse** — sea to land in summer, land to sea in winter. The SW monsoon is driven by the intense low over the heated Tibetan plateau and a permanent high east of **Madagascar**. Its **onset** is controlled by the Subtropical Jet Stream (STJ), the Tropical Easterly Jet (TEJ) and the ITCZ; its **intensity** by the Somali (**Findlater**) jet, the Somali current, the Indian Ocean branch of the **Walker** cell and the IOD. In winter the westerly STJ is split by the Himalaya–Tibet; the stronger southern branch (about **240** km/h) blows along about **25°N** and keeps the north dry. In late May–June it jumps north of Tibet and the monsoon can **burst** within days. The TEJ then blows east to west at **6–9 km** between **5–20°N** till early October. If heavy **snow** lies on Tibet, heating is delayed, the easterly jet is weak and so is the monsoon. The Findlater current causes **upwelling** off the **Horn of Africa**.

**IOD and EQUINOO:** the Indian Ocean Dipole is the SST difference between a **western pole** (Arabian Sea) and an eastern pole south of **Indonesia**; it builds from April–May and peaks around October. A positive IOD (warm west) helps the Indian monsoon. **EQUINOO** is its atmospheric twin.

**Rhythm of the year:** IMD's four seasons are the **cold weather** (Dec–Feb), hot weather (Mar–May), SW monsoon (Jun–Sep) and **retreating monsoon** (Oct–Nov). The monsoon reaches Kerala around **1 June** and covers India by about **8 July**. The **Arabian Sea branch** is stronger; the Bay branch turns west along the Himalaya. A **break** comes when the **monsoon trough** shifts to the foothills. After the retreat comes the humid "**October heat**". India averages about 118–125 cm of rain, about **75%** from the SW monsoon.

| Local phenomenon | What and where |
|---|---|
| **loo** | hot dry summer wind of the northern plains |
| **mango showers** | pre-monsoon showers in Kerala–Karnataka (help mangoes) |
| cherry blossom showers | Karnataka coffee areas |
| **Kal Baisakhi** (Nor'westers) | violent evening storms of Bengal; "Bardoli Chheerha" in Assam (tea, jute) |
| western disturbances | from the **Mediterranean**; winter rain for **rabi** wheat |
| cyclones | mostly from the **Bay of Bengal**; **Oct**–Nov cyclones strike the east coast |

**Regional contrasts:** about **60%** of India lies north of the Tropic of Cancer, yet the climate is tropical monsoon. The Himalaya keep north India **3°C**–**8°C** warmer in winter. **Mawsynram** and Cherrapunji get about 1,100 cm (**funnelling** plus orographic lift); Jaisalmer rarely 12 cm. The highest **diurnal** range is in the Thar and the highest **annual range** in the Himalaya. The **Coromandel** coast is dry in **July**–August and wet in Oct–Dec. The Arabian Sea branch blows **parallel to the Aravalli**, so Rajasthan stays dry; interior Deccan lies in the **rain shadow** of the Western Ghats.

**Köppen climates:** **Amw** (Goa/Konkan coast), As (Coromandel), Aw (savanna, most of the Peninsula), **BWhw** (hot desert, west Rajasthan), BShw (semi-arid), Cwg (Ganga plain), Dfc and E (Himalaya).

**Don't confuse**
STJ south of the Himalaya = no monsoon; STJ north of Tibet = onset. Positive IOD helps; El Niño hurts. Mango showers (Kerala) vs Kal Baisakhi (Bengal).

**TL;DR**
- Onset: STJ shift, TEJ, ITCZ; intensity: Somali jet, Walker cell, IOD; Tibetan snow → weak monsoon.
- Seasons: cold, hot, SW monsoon, retreating; Kerala ~1 June, all-India ~8 July.
- Loo, mango showers, Kal Baisakhi, western disturbances; Mawsynram wettest; Coromandel dry in July.
keyPoints: The southern branch of the Subtropical Jet blows along about 25°N in winter and must shift north of Tibet for the monsoon to burst.
The Tropical Easterly Jet (5–20°N, 6–9 km) blows east to west during the monsoon; heavy Tibetan snow leads to a weak monsoon.
The IOD compares a western pole (Arabian Sea) with an eastern pole south of Indonesia; EQUINOO is its atmospheric component.
Western disturbances from the Mediterranean bring winter rain for rabi crops; mango showers and Kal Baisakhi are pre-monsoon storms.
IMD seasons: cold weather, hot weather, SW monsoon, retreating monsoon; the monsoon reaches Kerala about 1 June.

items.title: Soils of India — ICAR Groups, Properties and Where They Occur
items.body:
### Soils of India — ICAR Groups, Properties and Where They Occur

**In one line**
Each Indian soil reflects its parent rock and its rainfall: learn colour, what it is rich/poor in, the crop, and the region.

**The story**
**Pedology** is the study of soils; **pedogenesis** is soil formation by weathering, leaching and calcification. Soil depends on **parent rock**, climate, relief, natural vegetation and time. A soil profile shows layers called **horizon**s. ICAR groups Indian soils into **eight** classes.

| Soil | Properties | Where / crops |
|---|---|---|
| Alluvial (~43%) | light to **ash grey**; potash-rich, **phosphorus**-poor; Bhangar (old) and Khadar (new); sandier in the west | northern plains, deltas; wheat, rice, **maize**, sugarcane |
| Black (regur) | clayey; rich in iron, lime, calcium, potash, aluminium, **magnesium**; poor in **nitrogen**, phosphorus, humus; swells when wet, cracks when dry (**self-ploughing**) | Deccan lava — Maharashtra, **Malwa**, **Saurashtra**, western MP, Telangana/AP valleys; cotton |
| Red ("**omnibus** group") | crystalline rocks in low rain; red from **ferric oxide**, yellow when hydrated; porous, **friable**; no kankar; poor in lime, N, P, humus | **Tamil Nadu**, Karnataka, AP, Odisha, **Chhattisgarh**, Jharkhand; millets, pulses, groundnut |
| Laterite | Latin "**later**" = **brick**; intense **leaching** of lime and silica; rich in iron and **aluminium**; poor in N, K, lime, humus | Kerala, Karnataka, TN hills, Odisha, Assam, Meghalaya; **cashew**, **tapioca**, rubber, tea, coffee |
| Forest / mountain (~**8.7%**) | humus-rich, **acidic**, silty-loamy | Himalaya, Ghats; tea, coffee, fruit |
| Desert | wind-laid sand; high **soluble salts**, phosphate, calcium; low moisture, N | Rajasthan, N Gujarat; **bajra**, barley with irrigation |
| Saline-alkaline (**usar**, reh, kallar, thur) | salt crust; infertile | W Gujarat, Sundarbans, over-irrigated Punjab–Haryana; reclaimed with **gypsum** |
| Peaty / marshy | high organic matter, waterlogged | deltas, Kerala (**Kuttanad**), Uttarakhand; rice, **jute** |

**Erosion and conservation:** **gully** erosion cuts ravines (Chambal); sheet erosion removes topsoil evenly. Contour ploughing, terracing, strip cropping and **shelter belts** check it.

**Don't confuse**
Red soil forms in LOW rainfall on crystalline rock; laterite forms in HEAVY rainfall by leaching. Black soil is poor in nitrogen; alluvial is poor in phosphorus. Laterite is NOT found in Rajasthan.

**TL;DR**
- ICAR: 8 groups; alluvial largest (~43%).
- Black: self-ploughing, poor N/P; red: omnibus, ferric oxide; laterite: "later" = brick, leached, cashew/tapioca.
- Saline: usar/reh/kallar, gypsum; peaty: Kuttanad; forest soils acidic.
keyPoints: ICAR divides Indian soils into eight groups; alluvial is the most extensive.
Black soil is rich in lime, iron and magnesium but poor in nitrogen and phosphorus, and is self-ploughing.
Red soil is the "omnibus group", red from ferric oxide, and forms on crystalline rock in low rainfall.
Laterite (Latin "later" = brick) forms by intense leaching; it suits cashew and tapioca.
Saline-alkaline (usar/reh/kallar) soils are reclaimed with gypsum; peaty soils occur in Kuttanad (Kerala).

items.title: Natural Vegetation — Forest Types, Trees, Policy and ISFR 2023
items.body:
### Natural Vegetation — Forest Types, Trees, Policy and ISFR 2023

**In one line**
Rainfall and height decide India's forest types; learn each type's rainfall band, region and signature trees, plus the policy targets and the latest forest-cover numbers.

**The story**
NCERT groups the vegetation into tropical evergreen, deciduous (moist and dry), thorn/desert, **montane** and **tidal** (mangrove) forests. India has about **45,000** plant species and **91,000** animal species. The deciduous (monsoon) forests are the most widespread; their trees **shed** leaves in the dry season and teak dominates.

| Type | Rain / place | Trees and features |
|---|---|---|
| Tropical evergreen | > 200 cm; Western Ghats, NE, **Andaman**s, Terai | **multi-layered**; rosewood, **mahogany**, ebony, **garjan**, bamboo |
| Moist deciduous | 100–200 cm; Ghats' eastern slopes, Chhattisgarh, Odisha, E UP | teak, sal, **shisham**, arjun, **mahua**, bamboo |
| Dry deciduous | 70–100 cm; central India, rain shadow of the Ghats | teak, khair, **axlewood**, **tendu**, palash, bel, neem |
| Thorn / semi-desert | < 50 cm; Gujarat, Rajasthan, Punjab | acacia, **babul**, khejri, **Indian wild date**; long roots, fleshy stems |
| Montane | Himalaya, by height | sal/teak foothills → oak, chestnut → pine, **deodar**, fir, spruce → **rhododendron**, juniper → alpine grass |
| Tidal (mangrove) | deltas | sundari, **hogla**, **garan**, pasur |

**Alpine pastures** are **bugyal**s in Uttarakhand and **marg**s (Gulmarg, Sonamarg) in Kashmir. **Mangrove belts:** Ganga (Sundarbans), Mahanadi (**Bhitarkanika**), Godavari–Krishna (**Coringa**, AP) and Cauvery (Pichavaram).

**Policy and cover:** the first National Forest Policy came in **1952**; the 1988 policy aims at 33% cover (**two-thirds** in the hills), checking erosion and desert spread, **social forestry** and a people's movement with women. **ISFR 2023** (released December 2024): forest cover **21.76**% and forest-plus-tree cover **25.17**%; by area **Madhya Pradesh** leads, then **Arunachal** Pradesh and Chhattisgarh; mangrove cover about **4,992** km², largest in West Bengal.

**Don't confuse**
Sal = moist deciduous; khair/tendu = dry deciduous; garjan = evergreen; babul = thorn. Bugyal (Uttarakhand) vs marg (Kashmir). 33% is the 1988 target, not the present cover (21.76%).

**TL;DR**
- Evergreen > 200 cm (garjan, mahogany); moist deciduous 100–200 (sal, shisham, mahua); dry 70–100 (tendu, axlewood); thorn < 50 (babul).
- Montane zones up to rhododendron and alpine bugyals/margs; mangroves at Sundarbans, Bhitarkanika, Coringa.
- Policy 1952, 1988 (33%, two-thirds hills); ISFR 2023 forest 21.76%, total 25.17%; MP largest.
keyPoints: Tropical evergreen forests (over 200 cm) are multi-layered, with mahogany, ebony and garjan.
Moist deciduous forests have sal, teak, shisham and mahua; dry deciduous forests have teak, khair, tendu and axlewood.
Alpine pastures are called bugyals in Uttarakhand and margs in Kashmir.
The 1988 National Forest Policy targets 33% forest cover (two-thirds in the hills).
ISFR 2023: forest cover 21.76%, forest plus tree cover 25.17%; Madhya Pradesh has the largest forest area.

**The story**
National parks are the strictest protected areas: fixed boundaries, no grazing or private rights; they cannot be **downgraded** to sanctuaries, and their boundaries change only by a resolution of the **state legislature**. items.body:
### Sanctuaries, Tiger Reserves and Protected-Area Records

**In one line**
Beyond national parks, India protects wildlife in sanctuaries and tiger reserves; the exam asks for counts, records and the rules that separate the categories.

**The story**
Sanctuaries and parks are declared under the Wildlife (Protection) Act, **1972**; sanctuaries are IUCN **Category IV** and allow some regulated activity. India has about **573** sanctuaries (Nov 2023) covering about 3.76% of its area. The largest is the **Kutch Desert** Wildlife Sanctuary (Gujarat, home of the wild ass); the oldest bird sanctuary is **Vedanthangal** (Tamil Nadu, protected since 1798). Keoladeo hosts over **370** bird species; our source calls **Rani Jhansi Marine** NP the largest marine sanctuary.

**Tiger reserves:** Project Tiger (1973) began with 9 reserves; each reserve has a **core** (national park/sanctuary) and a **buffer** (multiple-use zone) and is supervised by the statutory NTCA. India had **58** reserves by 2025 (Ratapani 57th, **Madhav** 58th, both MP). **Nagarjunasagar**–Srisailam (AP) is the **largest tiger reserve**. The 2022 estimate was at least **3,167** tigers (mean **3,682**) — about 75% of the world's wild tigers, with Madhya Pradesh first.

**Other species programmes:** Project Elephant (February **1992**); the elephant became the **National Heritage Animal** in 2010. The cheetah, extinct since **1952**, was brought to **Kuno** from Namibia in September 2022. The Asiatic lion lives wild only in **Gir**.

**Notable sanctuaries:** **Udanti** (wild buffalo, Chhattisgarh), National Chambal (gharial), **Askot** (musk deer, Uttarakhand), Pitti (birds, Lakshadweep). In AP: **Coringa** (mangroves), Kolleru, Pulicat, **Rollapadu** (great Indian bustard), Nelapattu (pelicans), Papikonda.

**Don't confuse**
Largest tiger reserve = Nagarjunasagar–Srisailam (AP), not the Sundarbans. Sanctuaries can be upgraded to national parks, never the reverse. WPA = 1972.

**TL;DR**
- ~106 NPs (1.3%); ~573 sanctuaries (3.76%); WPA 1972.
- Largest sanctuary Kutch Desert; oldest bird sanctuary Vedanthangal; largest TR Nagarjunasagar–Srisailam.
- 58 TRs by 2025 (Madhav 58th); tigers 3,167 (2022); Project Elephant 1992; cheetah to Kuno 2022.
keyPoints: National parks cannot be downgraded to sanctuaries; their boundaries change only by a state legislature resolution.

Nagarjunasagar–Srisailam (Andhra Pradesh) is India's largest tiger reserve.

items.title: Biosphere Reserves of India
items.body:
### Biosphere Reserves of India

**In one line**
India has **18 biosphere** reserves, notified from 1986 (Nilgiri) to 2011 (Panna); a dozen-plus are on UNESCO's Man and Biosphere (MAB) list.

**The story**
A biosphere reserve protects **whole ecosystems** together with the people living in its outer zones — unlike a sanctuary, which mainly protects animals. It has a strictly protected core zone, a **buffer zone** for research and education, and a **transition zone** of settlements and farms. Twelve Indian reserves were on the UNESCO list by 2020 (Panna last); in 2025 UNESCO added the **Cold Desert** reserve as the 13th.

| Reserve | Year | State | Note |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Nilgiri** | **1986** | TN, Kerala, Karnataka | first BR; UNESCO 2000 |
| **Nanda Devi** | 1988 | **Uttarakhand** | UNESCO 2004 |
| **Nokrek** | 1988 | Meghalaya (**Garo** Hills) | UNESCO 2009 |
| **Great Nicobar** | 1989 | A&N Islands | UNESCO 2013; sea-level |
| **Gulf of Mannar** | 1989 | Tamil Nadu | largest **marine** BR; UNESCO 2001 |
| **Manas BR** | 1989 | **Assam** |  |
| **Sundarban** | 1989 | **West Bengal** | Ganga–Brahmaputra delta, West Bengal; UNESCO 2001 |
| **Simlipal** | 1994 | Odisha (**Mayurbhanj**) | UNESCO 2009 |
| **Dibru**-Saikhowa | 1997 | Assam (Dibrugarh, **Tinsukia**) | smallest BR (MoEFCC; source says Nokrek) |
| **Dehang**-Dibang | 1998 | **Arunachal** Pradesh |  |
| **Pachmarhi** | 1999 | MP (Betul, **Hoshangabad**, Chhindwara) | UNESCO 2009 |
| **Khangchendzonga** | 2000 | Sikkim | **highest** BR; UNESCO 2018 |
| **Agasthyamalai** | 2001 | Tamil Nadu, **Kerala** | UNESCO 2016 |
| **Achanakmar**-Amarkantak | 2005 | MP, **Chhattisgarh** | UNESCO 2012 |
| **Kachchh** | 2008 | Gujarat | **largest** BR by area (MoEFCC) |
| **Cold Desert** | 2009 | Himachal (Pin Valley, Chandratal, **Kibber**) | UNESCO 2025 |
| **Seshachalam** Hills | 2010 | Andhra Pradesh (Tirupati, Kadapa) | Eastern Ghats; **red sanders** |
| **Panna** | 2011 | Madhya Pradesh | UNESCO **2020** |

**Don't confuse**
Largest BR = Kachchh (MoEFCC list) — the source text says Gulf of Mannar, which is the largest MARINE one. Smallest = Dibru-Saikhowa (MoEFCC) — source says Nokrek. Seshachalam is AP's biosphere reserve (red sanders).

**TL;DR**
- 18 BRs; first Nilgiri 1986; last Panna 2011; UNESCO 12 + Cold Desert (2025).
- Zones: core, buffer, transition.
- Kachchh largest, Gulf of Mannar largest marine, Khangchendzonga highest, Seshachalam (AP) red sanders.
keyPoints: India has 18 biosphere reserves; Nilgiri (1986) was the first.
Biosphere reserves have core, buffer and transition zones.
Seshachalam Hills BR (2010) in the Eastern Ghats of Andhra Pradesh protects red sanders.
Gulf of Mannar is the largest marine biosphere reserve; Khangchendzonga the highest.
Cold Desert BR (Himachal) was added to UNESCO's MAB list in 2025.

items.title: For Mains — Physical Geography of India (and AP)
items.body:
This topic feeds **Mains Paper-II** (clauses M2-11 "physical features & resources of India & AP" and M2-14 "fauna & floral geography"). Mains wants the **significance and interlinkages** of relief, drainage, climate, soils and vegetation — not a list of peaks.

## Dimensions Mains asks

| Dimension | What to write |
|---|---|
| Relief → economy | Himalayas (perennial rivers, hydropower, defence), plains (foodgrain bowl), plateau (minerals, cotton soil), coasts (ports, fisheries) |
| Drainage | Himalayan (perennial, antecedent, floods) vs Peninsular (seasonal); interlinking and water disputes |
| Climate | monsoon dependence, El Niño/IOD, uneven rainfall, drought/flood duality |
| Soils & vegetation | soil–crop link; forest cover (ISFR), 33% target; biodiversity hotspots (Western Ghats) |
| AP significance | eastern Deccan margin, Eastern Ghats (Arma Konda ~1,680 m), about 974 km east coast, Godavari–Krishna deltas, cyclone exposure |

## Data, reports and committees to quote
- **India State of Forest Report (ISFR 2023)** for forest-cover trends; the **1988 National Forest Policy** 33% target.
- **Western Ghats** as a UNESCO World Heritage biodiversity hotspot; the **Gadgil/Kasturirangan** reports on its protection.
- **Project Tiger (1973)/NTCA**; new tiger reserves and Ramsar wetland additions (Kolleru, Pulicat in AP).
- Monsoon dependence: a large share of the net sown area is still rain-fed.

## The AP angle
AP's physiography — the Eastern Ghats, the eastern Deccan plateau and the emergent delta coast — explains its paddy-and-aquaculture economy, its reliance on the north-east monsoon, and its vulnerability to Bay of Bengal cyclones and coastal erosion.

## Use in answers
- **Example:** link the Godavari–Krishna deltas and alluvial soil to AP's rice bowl and shrimp exports.
- **Quote/frame:** "relief sets the stage, climate writes the script, and soils decide the harvest."
- **Diagram idea:** a labelled sketch-map of the six physiographic divisions, or a flow line relief → drainage → soil → crop.
keyPoints: Serves Mains Paper-II (M2-11 physical features & resources; M2-14 fauna & flora).
Argue interlinkages: relief → drainage → climate → soils → crops, not isolated facts.
Quote ISFR 2023, the 33% forest target, Western Ghats hotspot (Gadgil/Kasturirangan), Project Tiger.
AP angle: Eastern Ghats, eastern Deccan margin, about 974 km delta coast, cyclone exposure.
Use a six-divisions sketch-map and the relief→crop flow as answer value-adds.
